May 2000A note about the UNDAF
The UNDAF is a strategic planning and collaborative programming framework that helps to identify priorities
for United Nations action. It is a key component of the UN Secretary-General's reform proposal of July 1997.
The UNDAF is designed to bring greater coherence, collaboration and effectiveness to United Nations
development efforts in the field in order to improve the well-being of the people served by the organization.
In short, the UNDAF identifies for the UN system organizations working in Cambodia: common challenges,
common responses, common resource frameworks, etc.
Through the UNDAF preparation process, the UNCT has resolved that the development challenges facing
Cambodia could best be jointly addressed by the UN system organizations by grouping their programmatic
and other activities under four mutually supportive areas of concentration and a total of 16 components.
Choices made for the UNDAF are based on the challenges faced by the country, on the Royal Government
of Cambodia priorities in meeting these challenges, and on the comparative advantages of the UN system in
Cambodia. The Common Country Assessment (CCA), produced by the UN system in 1998 pinpointed
critical concerns and challenges facing Cambodia, particularly in the areas addressed at the major global
UN conferences of the 1990s, and was used a stepping stone for the preparation of the UNDAF.
The UNDAF is not a programme in itself but a frame of reference within which the UN System organizations
in Cambodia will work with the national authorities over the next five years. It will also be used as a platform
for ongoing 'policy dialogue' with the Government and development partners. It provides a perspective on
how UN system organizations intend to address jointly identified challenges in a holistic and coherent
manner. By endorsing the UNDAF, participating UN organizations agree to support, through their respective
country programmes, the achievement of the objectives and development outcomes identified in each
component of the UNDAF.
The UNDAF should be considered a process fostering cooperation among UN system organizations rather
than just a product. Through the UNDAF, the UN system will improve programmatic coherence and
enhance the impact and effectiveness of its assistance. The UNDAF will be regularly reviewed, taking into
consideration progress made in achieving the objectives through country programmes of individual UN
organizations. The process thus intends to be iterative, with feedback between the programming instruments
of UN organizations and the UNDAF.
Content of the UNDAF Document
Section One, "Rationale", provides a brief presentation and explanation of the particular choices made in
the UNDAF from the broader set of issues identified in the CCA. It indicates how these choices respond to
national needs and priorities and, taking into account past performance of the UN system in Cambodia, how
they are likely to increase the impact of UN system cooperation. It also highlights the contribution of the
UNDAF to the improvement of follow-up to UN conferences and the support of the implementation of
conventions and declarations.
Section Two, "Goals and Objectives", provides a brief presentation of the situation to be addressed in
each area of concentration and component of UN system assistance and presents the goals and objectives
that will be pursued by UN system organizations. For each component it details the expected results of the
UN system assistance ('development outcomes'), the type of assistance the UN system organizations
intends to proved as well as the implementation and cooperation modalities of this assistance. Section Two
also indicates how the UN System will address a series of crosscutting issues through their programme of
assistance.
Section Three, "Cooperation Strategies", indicates how the UN system proposes to achieve the
objectives of the UNDAF. It indicates the principles to be followed for implementing the provisions of the
UNDAF as well as how crosscutting issues are going to be integrated into UN system support and how
partnerships will be strengthened. It complements section 2 that provides details on the implementation
modalities to attain the objective and development outcomes of each UNDAF component.
Section Four, "Implementation, Follow-up and Review", provides a brief presentation and explanation of
the particular choices made in the UNDAF from the broader set of issues identified in the CCA. It indicates
how these choices respond to national needs and priorities and, taking into account past performance of the
UN system in Cambodia, how they are likely to increase the impact of UN system cooperation. It also
highlights the contribution of the UNDAF to the improvement of follow-up to UN conferences and the support
of the implementation of conventions and declarations.
Section Five, "Resources Framework", gives an indication of the resources available to implement the
UNDAF and the relation between availability of resources and the choices of objectives and development
outcomes."Which countries will succeed in mobilizing

"Together, we can make a difference"
We, the United Nations Country Team in Cambodia, are committed to supporting the
development goals of the country. Contributing to the social and economic development of
Cambodia, we will promote participatory and people-centered development to achieve the
national goals of reducing extreme poverty and fostering human development. We will contribute
through our activities to the respect and fulfillment of the rights of the people of Cambodia,
including their right to social and economic development.
Through the preparation of the United Nations Development Assistance Framework, we have
developed a common response to the development challenges of the country. This response
takes into consideration national priorities, as well as the comparative advantages and
experience of our organizations in Cambodia. We agree that from 2001 to 2005 we will
contribute: to strengthening good governance; to building an environment for peace, justice and
development; to reducing extreme poverty; to achieving a better quality of life for all Cambodians;
and to the sustainable management of natural resources. We will work to strengthen national
capacities and contribute to the creation of an environment which enables the achievement of
these objectives.
While supporting national goals, we are committed to continuing to work in partnership with the
broader development community, including all parts of the Royal Government of Cambodia,
bilateral and multilateral donors, non-governmental organizations, civil society and the private
sector. We see the UNDAF as a tool that fosters policy dialogue between the UN system and the
Government of Cambodia and between the UN system and the development community.
While respecting the specific identities and mandates of our organizations, we are committed to
achieving programmatic coherence and mutual reinforcement to enhance the impact and
effectiveness of our assistance, through UN system-wide goal-oriented collaboration. In that
respect, the UNDAF indicates the objectives which our contributions will help to achieve and the
support we will provide to Cambodia.TABLE OF CONTENT

Executive Summary

UNDAF EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. RATIONALE
Based on the findings of the Common Country Assessment1 (CCA) and on the mandates,
experience and comparative advantages of UN system organizations working in Cambodia,
the UN Country Team (UNCT) identified the areas of development in which the UN system
should concentrate its efforts during the UNDAF cycle.
The CCA clearly identified the eradication of poverty as the main challenge facing the country.
To effectively address this challenge the assessment identified that adoption of a holistic
approach based on the “linkages between illiteracy, poverty, environmental degradation,
population growth, child schooling, health and nutrition” would have a greater effect than
addressing each problem individually. The CCA resolved that supporting human development
should clearly be at the fore of any poverty eradication strategy in Cambodia to ensure that
economic growth benefits the whole population and brings about greater equality.
To contribute to the reduction of poverty, while ensuring that people are at the center of the
development process, has therefore been identified as the major challenge that should be
addressed by the UN system. As a precondition for the successful implementation of people
centered policies and activities, supporting good governance has also been identified as a
priority area of intervention as well as contributing to equal access to natural resources by
rural communities in order to ensure intergenerational equity.
The UNCT has resolved that these challenges could best be jointly addressed by the UN
system organizations by grouping their programmatic and other activities under four mutually
supportive areas of concentration and a total of 16 components. In addition, the UNCT has
identified a series of issues that, because of their crosscutting nature, will be addressed in all
areas of concentration. Choices made for the UNDAF are based on the challenges faced by
the country, on the Royal Government of Cambodia (RGC) priorities in meeting these
challenges, and on the comparative advantages of the UN system in Cambodia.

Section 1 - Rationale
ii
The UN system is uniquely placed to address in a comprehensive and coherent manner the
various determinants and facets of poverty and human development in Cambodia. Drawing
from its experience in community and institutional development at provincial and local levels,
the UN system can continue to play a valuable role in supporting the development of
appropriate policies at the national level and strengthening the capacities of national
institutions at central and local levels to implement these policies. Through its partnership with
the Government, the UN can contribute significantly to the reduction of poverty by playing a
supportive and catalytic role to mobilize the energies and resources of all development actors,
including the poor themselves.
Both the RGC and the donor community have recognized the positive role played so far by
the UN system in Cambodia in all four areas of concentration. Over the years, UN system
organizations have established a trustworthy relationship with the RGC with a view of
strengthening its capacities to address issues of governance, poverty, human development
and management of natural resources. The donor community has consistently provided
financial support to the activities of the UN system in these same areas. Through the UNDAF,
UN system organizations will work more closely together and address challenges in these
areas in a more comprehensive, coherent and cost-effective way.
The pooling of efforts of the UN system will also facilitate the integrated follow-up to the UN
global conferences that took place in the 1990s. The UN system will pursue policy dialogue
with the national authorities aimed at identifying nation-wide priority areas of concern based
on the global agenda developed through these conferences. It will aim at ensuring that this
agenda is properly addressed through national policies and programmes. The UNDAF will
also contribute to the coherent and coordinated implementation of the Secretary-General UN
action strategy for halving extreme poverty by 2015.
2. GOALS AND OBJECTIVES
As indicated above, the UN system contribution to the development of Cambodia will be
concentrated in four areas and a total of 16 components. Based on an analysis of the main
challenges in these areas and on national priorities, one goal of UN system assistance has
been identified for each area of concentration. It indicates the major development impact the
UN system, in cooperation with its partners, wants to contribute to in the medium to long
term,. It gives a sense of the broader context within which the UN system is working and of its
longer-term objectives. For each component, the UN system has agreed on one objective of
UN assistance indicating the specific contribution it intends to make to the achievement of the
goal for that area. In addition, the UN system has defined for each component a short list of
development outcomes (indicating the expected results of the assistance to be provided by
the UN system) and the implementation and cooperation modalities it intends to use to attain
these objectives. Only the goals and objectives are presented below.
2.1. Areas of concentration and components
Area of Concentration One: Governance, Peace and Justice
The UN system has resolved to concentrate its actions in support of good governance, peace
and justice around three components: rule of law; reform of the public administration; culture
of peace. This choice is based on the priorities expressed by the Government, the
comparative advantages of the UN system organizations in these sectors and on the
experience of the UN system in Cambodia in the past years. The strengthening of good
governance and the creation of an environment for peace and justice are absolute
prerequisites for any successful economic and social development efforts.
Goal
To build an environment for peace, justice and development by improving respect for
human rights, establishing the rule of law, improving public sector management and
strengthening social cohesion.UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005
Executive Summary
iii
Component 1.1.: Rule of law
The absence of the rule of law combined with a very weak capacity to administer justice
contributes to a climate of impunity, corruption and lack of respect of human rights. They also
impede the creation of a climate conducive to economic development and the efficient
implementation of development programmes. The intention of the UN system is thus to assist
the government in its stated aim of establishing the rule of law and upholding the human
rights of all the people of Cambodia, in accordance with the international human rights
conventions to which Cambodia has adhered.
Objective of UN system assistance
To promote the establishment of the rule of law through the strengthening of the capacity
and competence of the state institutions responsible for law-making, law enforcement
and the administration of justice, taking full account of the role and potential of civil
society to participate in these processes.
Component 1.2.: Public administration reform
Substantial efforts will be required in the years to come to build the capacities of the
government and of the public administration, especially in facing the challenges posed by the
modernization of the economy and by decentralization, and to implement reforms far-reaching
enough to encompass the required structural, managerial and behavioral changes. UN
system assistance will intervene in this area at two levels in a concerted and coherent
manner. On the one hand, it will build capacity inside the Secretariat of the Council of
Administrative Reform to support the government in the design, implementation and
coordination of a national public administration reform programme. In parallel, it will continue
to support the decentralization and deconcentration process and build capacities at the local
levels to face increased responsibilities.
Objective of UN system assistance
To strengthen capacities for the efficient and effective functioning of government
institutions and public administration at the central and local levels.
Component 1.3.: Culture of Peace
30 years of war and social turmoil in Cambodia have resulted in the destruction of trust and of
human capital. There is a compelling need for concerted efforts to create a peaceful and
harmonious environment through the promotion of greater social cohesion in Cambodia. The
many initiatives and activities already under way in this area would benefit from improved
coherence and greater integration. Working mainly at the grass-roots level and with a special
focus on children and youth, the UN system will promote and popularize the concept of
“culture of peace” to achieve that result.
Objective of UN system assistance
To strengthen social cohesion and to promote a culture of tolerance, non-violence,
respect for human rights and cultural pluralism among the population.
Area of Concentration Two: Poverty Reduction
An important reduction of poverty during the UNDAF cycle could happen if the country
experiences a strong economic growth and if this growth is well distributed among regions
and benefits the whole population. Through the UNDAF, the UN system will support the
Government initiatives in this respect. It will concentrate its poverty reducing efforts in the
poorest areas of the country while supporting the development of national policy initiatives
which influence the life of the poor. The contributions of the UN system to address the
challenge of poverty reduction in Cambodia will occur according to a four-way approach that
will:
• promote an enabling environment through poor sensitive policies and access to land;
• support the mobilization and organization of the poor;
• promote the livelihood of the poor by ensuring, inter alia, their access to productive
assets, employment, income generating opportunities and credit;
• improve the nutritional status of the population.UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005
Section 1 - Rationale
iv
Goal
To contribute to the reduction of overall poverty with particular emphasis in poorest
areas.
Component 2.1.: Enabling environment
The UN system will contribute to the establishment of an environment more conducive to
poverty reduction. It will do this by working at the policy level, supporting the development and
monitoring of anti-poverty programmes and the integration of population and gender concerns
into national policies. In conjunction with this the UN system will improve access to land and
facilitate reconstruction and area development activities through the implementation of a well
targeted mine action programme.
Objective of UN assistance:
To contribute to an enabling environment for poverty reduction through the development
of pro-poor policies and by improving safe access to land for the poor and vulnerable
groups.
Component 2.2.: Community development
Obstacles to community development and empowerment are immense. There continues to be
an urgent need for institutional development and capacity building to ensure that local
communities become key participators in the development process and contribute
substantially to poverty reduction. This need is emphasized by the gradual expansion of the
political space at community level through the planned commune elections and by the
Government’s intention to further decentralize the public administration and deconcentrate
responsibilities for planning, financing and management of development to lower levels of the
government structure.
Objective of UN assistance:
To support the development and empowerment of community institutions that enable
Cambodians, especially the poorer members of society, to identify and address their
own needs.
Component 2.3.: Promotion of sustainable livelihoods
The UN system will contribute to sustainable livelihoods according to a three-fold approach:
- it will content to the needs of transient and chronically poor through the development and
implementation of a food based safety net, combined with the design of a food security
strategy and the development of national disaster management capacities;
- it will support the strengthening of the rural economy, qualitative and quantitative
improvement in agricultural outputs of the poor farmers and the creation of alternative
sources of income for poor individuals;
- it will support programs to prevent transient food insecurity among particularly vulnerable
population that, in the past, have resulted in high levels of chronic malnutrition among
women and children. This is both a major cause and outcome of poverty.
Objective of UN assistance:
To promote improvement in the livelihoods of the poor by improving their access to
productive assets and income-generating opportunities and by addressing food
insecurity.
Component 2.4.: Reducing Malnutrition
The UN system will contribute to reducing malnutrition among the Cambodian people at both
the national or policy level and at the local level through support of local programmes
targeting the causes and effects of malnutrition, including micronutrient malnutrition.
Objective of UN assistance:
To actively support policies and programmes which reduce the prevalence of proteinenergy malnutrition, iodine deficiency disorders, vitamin A deficiency and iron deficiency
anemia in young children and in women of reproductive age.UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005
Executive Summary
v
Area of concentration three: Human development
The UN system will support the RGC to address both the low level of human development
and the internal disparities among regions. The purpose will be to empower all Cambodians
to fully develop their capabilities through greater and affordable access to good quality basic
social services (i.e., basic health care, reproductive health and birth spacing, education and
safe water); and to reduce disparities among Cambodians and among regions. In addition,
the UN system will support the government in its efforts to revitalize the richness of
Cambodia’s culture, as a means to create a greater sense of identity and unity among its
population.
Goal
To support the achievement of a higher level of quality of life for all Cambodians by
promoting education, literacy and cultural development, improving health status and
decreasing vulnerability towards HIV/AIDS.
Component 3.1.: HIV/AIDS
The HIV/AIDS epidemic is not seen solely as a public health concern and the RGC has
developed policies and strategies to address the challenges HIV/AIDS poses in a
comprehensive manner. However, national authorities are presently ill equipped to efficiently
respond to the epidemic. The UN system will strengthen and support the efforts of the RGC
and civil society to do so.
Objective of UN assistance:
To assist the Government in preventing the spread of HIV infection in Cambodia while
providing care and support for those infected and affected by the epidemic and
alleviating the socio-economic and human impact of the epidemic.
Component 3.2.: Health and water and sanitation
A high burden of disease, a weak health infrastructure and poor health knowledge and
practices at household level are the three most significant health problems facing Cambodia
today. Despite recent progress by RGC and their development partners in addressing the low
access to and quality of public health services, and the positive progress made in the control
of specific diseases, the reforms put in place to rehabilitate the system are not yet achieving
their anticipated results. The UN system intends to support the RGC addressing these
challenges.
Objective of UN assistance
To improve the health and nutritional status of the Cambodian population by assisting
the Government in improving access to quality health services and safe water and by
improving family health and nutrition knowledge and practices.
Component 3.3: Reproductive health
During the UNDAF cycle, the UN system will support reproductive health national efforts in
three areas of high priority: safe motherhood, especially reduction of maternal mortality; birth
spacing; RTIs/STDs and HIV/AIDS .
Objective of UN assistance
To assist the Government in improving the reproductive health conditions in Cambodia
through the provision of affordable, sustainable and user-oriented reproductive health
services as well as by improving the reproductive health knowledge of men, women and
adolescents.
Component 3.4.: Education
The UN system contributions in the education sector will concentrate on: strengthening the
capacities of the Government at all levels to improve the performance of the sector; improving
access to quality basic education (i.e., early childhood, primary and lower secondary levels);
expanding access to adult literacy, specifically of women; and responding to educational
needs of disadvantaged groups. The UN system organizations will joint efforts to increaseUNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005

vi
education opportunities for girls and to ensure that all Cambodians have equal access to
education regardless of their sex and of their economic and social status.
Objective of UN assistance:
To contribute to equitable access to quality education and learning opportunities for all
Cambodians.
Component 3.5.: Cultural development
The intention of the UN system is to support the Government’s endeavors in promoting the
cultural development of the nation and in coordinating international assistance provided to the
country to protect its national cultural heritage.
Objective of UN assistance:
To protect and promote the cultural heritage, tangible and intangible, of the
country.
Area of concentration four: Sustainable management of natural resources
The UN system will focus its contributions on supporting national efforts in the following four
areas: land use planning, forestry, fisheries, and environmental awareness and protection.
Together, these areas address the main concerns linked with sustainable management of
natural resources in Cambodia. The UN system strategy will be to work to preserve and
protect the natural resources and ecosystems of the country while promoting fair access to
natural resource assets for rural and community development.
Goal
To support development and implementation of policies and practices which contribute
to sustainable management of natural resources for local and rural development.
Component 4.1.: Land use
There is a very high risk of over-exploitation and deterioration of natural resources in
Cambodia in the present situation of excessive logging, deforestation, land grabbing,
uncontrolled fishing, non-regulated settling, rising demand for agricultural production, etc. .
This situation calls for the development of land use planning (covering the whole territory,
including forest, lakes and rivers) that will ensure long-term protection and sustainable
management of natural resources while maximizing economic and social benefits to
communities and society as a whole.
Objective of UN assistance
Contribute to long-term sustainable management of natural resources through the
development and implementation of integrated land use planning.
Component 4.2.: Forestry
Cambodian forests are increasingly at risk due to expanding demand for agricultural lands,
timber, and fuel wood because of rapidly increasing population coupled with accelerated
economic development. Current exploitation practices threaten the livelihoods of communities
living in or around forests plus there has been a perceived decrease in bio-diversity due to
habitat destruction. The UN System will support the consolidation of RGC’s reform measures
to suppress illegal forest activities and build a coherent policy in the sector. It will support the
implementation of appropriate conservation measures.
Objective of UN assistance
To strengthen capacities to conserve and manage forest resources and
ecosystems while maximizing the contribution of forestry to employment creation,
income generation, rural development, poverty reduction and economic growth.
Component 4.3.: Fisheries
Structural problems in the sector are raising growing concerns over the long-term productivity
of fishery resources as well as the contribution of fisheries to the livelihoods of small-scaleUNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005
Executive Summary
vii
fishermen and associated communities. It is the intention of the UN system to support
national authorities in addressing these concerns.
Objective of UN assistance
To promote productive, equitable and sustainable management of fishery resources
which supports local community development.
Component 4.4.: Environment awareness and protection
The necessity to protect Cambodia’s rich biological diversity is recognized by the Government
and efforts are being made to protect the country’s forest, wetland, marine and coastal
ecosystems. The UN System will continue to support these efforts and will contribute to
awareness raising to ensure that appropriate policies are developed and implemented for the
protection of these ecosystems. Special emphasis will be on protecting the Tonle Sap Lake’s
unique ecosystem.
Objective of UN assistance
To support the conservation of Cambodia’s unique ecosystems and to promote safe
disposal of solid waste.
2.2. Crosscutting issues
In addition to these areas of concentration and components presented above, the UNCT
identified seven crosscutting issues that cannot be comprehensively addressed through any
specific component or area of concentration. To be effectively addressed, these issues need
to be systematically integrated into many, if not all, of the UNDAF areas and components.
The crosscutting issues are: i) human rights; ii) gender equality and empowerment of women;
iii) minority groups; iv) children and youths’ rights; v) participation and democracy; vi) regional
cooperation; and vii) reintegration of demobilized soldiers.
Where relevant, these issues have been addressed in the plan of actions developed for each
of the components presented above. As indicated in 3.3. their integration into the
programmes of participating organizations and the global UN response to these issues will be
monitored by the UNDAF Monitoring Working Group.
3. COOPERATION STRATEGIES
The UN system proposes to achieve UNDAF’s objectives by providing assistance for capacity
development, by promoting national execution, by increasingly targeting its assistance and by
promoting the use of a sector wide and programme approach.
3.1. Implementation modalities
Capacity development
Capacity development will be the main thrust of the UN system assistance to Cambodia.
Emphasis will continue to be put on building or strengthening the capacities and skills of
national institutions and local organizations to efficiently develop and implement policies and
programmes supporting the development process of the country. Both the RGC and the UN
system recognize that a significant programme of reforms have to be implemented or
consolidated in the four areas of concentration covered by the UNDAF. The capacities of the
institutions and organizations mandated to develop and implement these reforms at the
central and local level still need to be consolidated to ensure their success.

Section One RATIONALE
The areas where the UN system should concentrate its efforts during the UNDAF cycle have
been identified by the UN Country Team in (UNCT) Cambodia through the Common Country
Assessment (CCA) for Cambodia1. The CCA’s objective was to pinpoint critical concerns and
challenges facing Cambodia, in particular in the areas addressed at the major global UN
conferences of the 1990s. Based on this analysis, the CCA identified areas requiring priority
attention in development cooperation.
The CCA highlights the multiple dimensions and determinants of poverty and clearly identifies the
eradication of poverty as the main challenge facing the country. The linkages between poverty
and macro-economic policies, governance, literacy, schooling, access to health services, food
security, etc. are explored and documented in the CCA. The reciprocal relationships between
poverty and environmental degradation are identified.
The CCA also makes a preliminary identification of interventions that would contribute to poverty
reduction and underlines that adoption of a holistic approach based on the “linkages between
illiteracy, poverty, environmental degradation, population growth, child schooling, health and
nutrition” would have a greater effect than addressing each problem individually. The CCA
resolved that supporting human development should clearly be at the fore of any poverty
eradication strategy in Cambodia.
Around 36% of the Cambodian population were living below the income-poverty line in 1998. But
at the same time, income poverty is relatively shallow and it is estimated that a reduction of 50%
could occur through sustained economic growth over a period of 5 to 8 years2. However, for this
to happen, certain conditions need to be met. If the proper conditions are not met, economic
growth could be accompanied by the over-exploitation and degradation of Cambodia’s natural
resources, an increase in inequalities among its citizens and greater imbalances between rural
and urban areas. This is a process by which some regions and economic classes would capture
all benefits accompanying growth while others would be neglected and continue to live in poverty
and even see their situation deteriorate.
The 1999 edition of the Cambodia Human Development Report also explored the linkages
between poverty, human development and economic growth. The report recognized that
“Cambodia has some of the worst human development indicators in Asia”3 and stressed that the
experience of other countries in the region (e.g. Sri Lanka, China, Thailand and Philippines)
indicates that improved human development is not automatically ensured by economic growth. All
the countries in Asia that have impressive human development indicators have implemented
direct policy interventions to improve health, schooling and literacy.
To contribute to the reduction of poverty while ensuring that people are at the center of the
development process has therefore been identified as the major challenge that should be
addressed by the UN system in Cambodia. Taking into consideration its past experience and its
comparative advantages vis-à-vis other development partners, the UN Country Team has
resolved that the UN system could best address this challenge through the UNDAF by grouping
their programmatic and other activities under four mutually supportive areas of concentration and
a total of 16 components as shown in the following schema.

AREA OF
CONCENTRATION ONE GOVERNANCE, PEACE AND JUSTICE
1. Context and rationale
Since the signature of the Paris Agreements, Cambodia has enjoyed sustained economic
growth and the Royal Government of Cambodia has made efforts at rebuilding the main
institutions of the State. Cambodia is also witnessing the emergence of a vibrant civil society
and of civil society organizations (CSOs) representing different segments of the population
and promoting their rights. For the first time in decades, the country is at peace.
This situation needs to be consolidated and sustained. After 30 years of conflict, the social
fabric is still weak and mistrust still exists at all levels in society. To ensure that the rights of
citizens are respected, both their civil and political rights as well as their economic and social
rights, an accountable, efficient and well-functioning public administration must be put in place
together with an appropriate legal framework. The participation of citizens and community in
national and local policy debates and in setting the course for their own social and economic
development has to be strengthened. Initial steps taken towards decentralization and
deconcentration should be supported. The strengthening of good governance and the
creation of an environment for peace and justice are absolute prerequisites for any successful
economic and social development efforts.
The Royal Government of Cambodia recognizes the need to establish the rule of law and to
improve public governance in all its aspects and to promote a fully participatory democracy
within which respect for human rights will be upheld. To achieve this, an effective legal
system based on well-designed and drafted laws and legal codes will be essential,
implemented by well-trained, experienced and appropriately-paid judicial and administrative
personnel. The reform and restructuring of the public administration to enable it to perform its
assigned duties in a market-oriented economy is also a high priority for the Government.
These needs and priorities were highlighted in the Royal Government Platform for the second
term (1998-2003) as well as in the presentation made at the Consultative Group meeting of
February 1999. The Government recognizes also that after decades of conflict, one of its
main challenges is to “rebuild national life” and to consolidate the achievements of the
process of national reconciliation which has begun in recent years.
The promotion of good governance was also identified through the CCA as a priority for the
development of the country. The CCA stressed the need to develop the capacity for good
governance as a “prerequisite for the sustainability of poverty eradication efforts in
Cambodia”. It stresses that the cornerstones for such an effort are: the reform of state
institutions; increased budgetary authority and decision-making at local level; the promotion of
basic human rights; and the establishment of the rule of law through the strengthening of the
judiciary.
The UN system has thus resolved to concentrate its actions in support of good governance,
peace and justice around three components: rule of law; reform of the public administration;
culture of peace. This choice is based on the comparative advantages of the UN system
organizations in these sectors and on the experience gained by the UN system in Cambodia
in the past years.
2. Goal of UN System assistance
To build an environment for peace, justice and development by improving respect for human
rights, establishing the rule of law and improving public sector management and
strengthening social cohesionUNDAF CAMBODIA 2001-2005

Component 1.1. Rule of law
The absence of the rule of law combined with a very weak capacity to administer justice
contribute to a climate of impunity, corruption and lack of respect of human rights. They also
impede the creation of a climate conducive to economic development and the efficient
implementation of development programmes. The intention of the UN system is thus to assist
the government in its stated aim of establishing the rule of law and upholding the human
rights of all the people of Cambodia, in accordance with the international human rights
conventions to which Cambodia has adhered.
Objective:
To promote the establishment of the rule of law through the strengthening of the
capacity and competence of the state institutions charged with law-making, law
enforcement and the administration of justice, taking full account of the role and
potential of civil society to participate in these processes
Development outcomes:
• An efficient and participatory law-making process making full use of the capacity of civil society are
in place, focusing on national legislative priorities related to the promotion of the rule of law and the
protection of vulnerable groups
• National and local capacities to implement laws effectively and in accordance with the rule of law
and human rights norms are built and independent capacity to monitor implementation are created
• Conditions exist for the functioning of an independent, well-trained and appropriately
regulated and compensated judiciary and the establishment of an autonomous
prosecution service is under way
• Civil society organizations are functioning freely and effectively to promote the basic civil,
political, economic, social and cultural rights of the population
Implementation and coordination modalities

benefiting the legislative institutions, the judiciary and court services, and law enforcement
bodies as well as NGOs and civil society organizations working in the sector. Capacitybuilding components will be defined in close collaboration with national authorities and
organizations making full use of national resources, including local NGOs.
Advocacy and policy dialogue will play an important role. Based on the different human rights
conventions Cambodia has adhered to, the UN system will continue advocating for promotion
and respect of human rights. The UN system will assist the Government in fulfilling its
reporting obligations to the human rights treaty bodies and in interpreting and promulgating
the recommendations of the bodies. The UN system will maintain policy dialogue with the
authorities to ensure that the reform of the judiciary and of law enforcement agencies
continue to be considered as priorities by the Government and are properly addressed. It will
also play a role in mobilizing support from the donor community to support these reform
processes.

Component 1.2. Public administration reform
The Royal Government of Cambodia has expressed its wish to transform the current public
administration into one more operational, more productive and more accountable, which
would be more efficient and effective in supporting economic and social development. The
Government also plans to hold commune elections and to implement a commune
administration law which would create commune councils with authority to raise revenue,
receive funding and manage local development. Substantial efforts will be required in the
years to come to build the capacities of the government and of the public administration to
face the challenges posed by the modernization of the economy and by decentralization.
Efforts will also be need to successfully implement reforms far-reaching enough to
encompass the required structural, managerial and behavioral changes, and to pursue the
fight against corruption.
UN system assistance will intervene in this area at two levels in a concerted and coherent
manner. It will build capacity inside the Secretariat of the Council of Administrative Reform
(CAR) to support the government in the design, implementation and coordination of a national
public administration reform programme. In parallel, it will continue to support the
decentralization and deconcentration10 process and build capacities at the local levels to face
increased responsibilities.

To strengthen capacities for the efficient and effective functioning of government
institutions and public administration at the central and local levels

AREA OF
CONCENTRATION TWO POVERTY REDUCTION
1. Context and rationale
With an estimated 36% of the overall population and 40% of the rural population living below
the poverty line in 1997, addressing poverty constitutes a critical challenge in Cambodia. The
challenge is also one of insuring that all Cambodians benefit from economic growth. As noted
in the CCA, while the number of poor has decreased slightly since 1993, from 39%, and the
per capita revenue has increased nation-wide, income distribution has worsened significantly.
The richest 20% of individuals experienced an increase in their relative share of national
consumption at the expense of the poorest 80%. In parallel, economic growth has been more
profitable to people living in urban areas then those in rural areas. Today, rural households
account for nearly 90% of Cambodia’s poor. Around 75% of the poor are self-employed.
Although poverty incidence is lower in urban areas, urban population growth could lead to an
increase in the number of urban poor.
Poverty in Cambodia has many determinants. Major among them are the lack of opportunity
for sustainable sources of income, the lack of access to productive assets such as land and
the low return on these assets because of the difficulty to access credit, the depleted rural
infrastructure, etc. Poverty in Cambodia is also a consequence of the low access to and high
cost of, particularly for the poor themselves, quality basic services such as education, health
and water. Determinants of poverty linked with access to basic social services will be
addressed through the human development section of the UNDAF (area of concentration 3).
The importance of fighting against poverty is fully recognized by the Royal Government of
Cambodia. The over-riding objective of Cambodia's first Socio-economic Development Plan
(1996-2000) was “the reduction and eventual eradication of poverty” and “speedy poverty
alleviation and economic progress”, was the most important agenda item of the 1998-2003
Royal Government platform issued in November 1998. To this date, Cambodia does not
have, however, a comprehensive national poverty reduction strategy.
In that context, the contributions of the UN system to address the challenge of reducing
poverty in Cambodia will follow a four-way approach that will:
• promote an enabling environment through poor sensitive policies and access to land;
• support the mobilization and organization of the poor;
• promote the livelihoods of the poor by ensuring, inter alia, their access to productive
assets, employment, income generating opportunities and credit;
• improve the nutritional status of the population.
An important reduction of poverty during the UNDAF cycle could happened if the country
experiences a strong economic growth and if this growth is well distributed among regions
and benefits the whole population. Through the UNDAF, the UN system will support the
Government initiatives in that respect. It will concentrate its efforts towards reducing poverty
in the poorest areas of the country while supporting the development of national policy
initiatives influencing the life of the poor. Geographical targeting will be an essential part of
UN system strategy in addressing poverty through its rural and community development
activities. The UN system will endeavor to agree on a priority list of areas of intervention and
to target the larger part of its assistance to these areas where the needs are most important.

Component 2.3. Promotion of sustainable livelihoods
UN system contributions to sustainable livelihoods will follow a three-fold approach. First, it
will content to the needs of chronically and transient poor through the development and
implementation of a food based safety net, combined with the design of a food security
strategy and the development of national disaster management capacities.

quantitative improvement in agricultural outputs of the poor farmers and the creation of
alternative sources of income for poor individuals. This takes into consideration the fact that
agriculture represents the main occupation of 75% of the population and that up to 40% of
this rural population lives below the poverty line and can only meet their basic needs with
great difficulty.
Thirdly, the UN system will support programs to prevent transient food insecurity among
particularly vulnerable population that, in the past, have resulted in high levels of chronic
malnutrition among women and children. This is both a major cause and outcome of poverty.

needs assessment, timely transfers, close monitoring of the end-use of commodities, and the

Component 2.4. Reducing malnutrition
Malnutrition in Cambodia is both a major cause and outcome of poverty and because it is relatively
widespread and unattended is considered a silent emergency. The UN system will contribute to
reducing malnutrition among the Cambodian people at the national or policy level and also at the local
level through support of local programmes targeting the causes and effects of malnutrition, including
micronutrient malnutrition.
There are many causes of malnutrition but its ties to poverty are strong. The economic returns to
reducing malnutrition are great, with huge gains in productivity, especially in the case of iron
deficiency anemia and iodine deficiency disorders. Malnutrition should not be equated with food
production alone but more with food access, access to adequate health care, immunization, education
on nutrition and health, child feeding and caring practices, access to reproductive health information
and services, and access to safe water and sanitation. These other issues are covered in the human
development section of this document and in the promotion of sustainable livelihoods component
(2.3).
UN system activities in terms of addressing malnutrition will be guided and implemented under the
general framework of the CNIP (1999-2008) as well as the final recommendations of the National
Seminar on Food Security and Nutrition that were adopted as RGC policy in May of 1999. From the
CNIP, the UN system will uphold the development of national policies and guidelines to address main
malnutrition disorders as well as the national ability for improved nutritional monitoring and planning.
In addition, they will work with the Council for Agricultural and Rural Development in implementing the
recommendations from the National Seminar on Food Security and Nutrition in order to reduce the
unacceptably high levels of acute and chronic malnutrition, iodine deficiency disorders (IDD), vitamin
A deficiency (VAD) and iron deficiency anemia (IDA) in the country.
Objective of UN assistance:
To actively support policies and programmes to reduce the prevalence of protein-energy
malnutrition, iodine deficiency disorders, vitamin A deficiency and iron deficiency anemia in young
children and in women of reproductive age.
Development outcomes
• Regular monitoring of the nutritional status of the population is conducted to provide nutrition
relevant information in support of community and national based strategies as well as to record
progress in reducing malnutrition in the country
• The prevalence of underweight and chronically malnourished children is reduced significantly,
indicating improved nutritional status for the entire population
• The high prevalence of malnutrition in women of reproductive age is reduced and levels of low
birth weight children (< 2500 g) are also significantly reduced
• More than 50% of households in Cambodia are using iodized salt, most of which is produced
locally
• There is universal distribution of vitamin A capsules to children 6 to 59 months, schools children,
pregnant and lactating women
• High distribution rates of iron supplements, and active de-worming campaigns help to reduce the
extremely high rates of iron deficiency anemia in young children and women, especially pregnant
women
Implementation modalities
The government’s already strong commitment to addressing nutrition issues is reflected in acceding to
the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), signing the CEDAW, adopting the recommendations
of the 1999 National Seminar on Food Security and Nutrition, and the endorsement of several World
Declarations addressing malnutrition, including the 1992 International Conference on Nutrition, and
the 1996 World Food Summit. Activities in this sector will be guided by the recommendations of these
Conferences. In addition to programmatic activities, the UN system will advocate to give adequate
attention and devote adequate resources to fight against malnutrition. Support will also be provided to
monitor progress made.UNDAF CAMBODIA 2001-2005

Context and rationale
Years of conflict and severe human and physical destruction have devastated Cambodia’s
human capital. Since the peace returned, efforts being made to rebuild the society are starting
to produce results, however such a task can only be accomplished over many years.
Cambodia has one of the lowest human development index (HDI) scores in Asia14. The HDI
also indicates significant disparities in human development among provinces, and more
particularly between urban and rural areas (the HDI score for urban Cambodia is nearly 25%
greater than for rural Cambodia) and across economic groups. The child risk measure
developed by UNICEF (reflecting risks a child faces until the age of 18), indicates that
Cambodian children face the highest risk in all of East and South Asia and the Pacific. These
“scores” reflect years of conflict, the weakness of social infrastructure and of the relatively low
level of education of the population. The high prevalence rate of HIV/AIDS in Cambodia
poses a major threat to development and predicted increases will lead to a deterioration of the
current human development situation.
In recent years, the RGC has made efforts to address this situation. In the health and
education sectors, it has initiated reform processes that are contributing to improved delivery
and quality of social services. National policies and strategies to address HIV/AIDS have
been developed. The government commitment to human development has been reiterated in
its platform for the second term (1998-2003). RGC has reiterated its intention to increase
public spending for the social sectors at the Consultative Group meeting of February 199915.
The UN system will support the RGC to address both the low level of human development
and the internal disparities among regions. The purpose will be to empower all Cambodians
to fully develop their capabilities through greater and affordable access to good quality basic
social services (i.e., basic health care, reproductive health and birth spacing, education and
safe water); and to reduce disparities among Cambodians and among regions. In addition,
the UN system will support the government in its efforts to revitalize the richness of
Cambodia’s culture, as a means to create a greater sense of unity among its population.
As stated in Section 1 (Rationale), the CCA has clearly indicated the strong linkages existing
in Cambodia between poverty and access to basic social services and the need to develop an
approach for poverty eradication that touch upon all these dimensions. In that sense, the
Human Development area of concentration, by strengthening capabilities of the Cambodian
people and contributing to better access to social services such as primary education, basic
health services (including reproductive health services) and water and sanitation facilities, will
substantially contribute to the reduction of poverty in Cambodia.

Component 3.1. HIV / AIDS
The HIV epidemic is well established in Cambodia and affects every province and every
population group. Cambodia has one of the highest levels of infection with HIV in Southeast
Asia. The impact of this epidemic on the future development of Cambodia will be profound, on
the people, on the economy and on all aspects of human development.
Based upon surveillance data collected from 18 provinces in 1998, the number of HIV
infections among Cambodians aged 15-49 years is 180,000. It is estimated each day a further
one hundred new infections occur. Estimates predict that by the year 2000 there will be
11,000 people with AIDS and by 2005 there will be 25,000.
It is important that this epidemic is not seen solely as a public health concern and to
acknowledge that the RGC has developed policies and strategies to address the challenges
HIV/AIDS poses in a comprehensive manner. However, national authorities are presently ill
equipped to efficiently respond to the epidemic. The UN system will strengthen and support
the efforts of the RGC and civil society to do so.

To assist the Government in preventing the spread of HIV infection in Cambodia while
providing care and support for those infected and affected by the epidemic and
alleviating the socio-economic and human impact of the epidemic

Component 3.2. Health and Water and Sanitation
A high burden of disease, a weak health infrastructure and poor health knowledge and
practices at household level are the three most significant health problems facing Cambodia
today. They result in the health status of the Cambodian people being one of the lowest in
Southeast Asia. Despite recent progress by RGC and their development partners in
addressing the low access to and quality of public health services, and the progress made in
the control of specific diseases, the reforms put in place to rehabilitate the system are not yet
achieving their anticipated results. The health sector is seriously under-funded and it is
estimated that only one third of the necessary structures are in place. Staff allocation is not
yet related to need, health workers skills are not adequate and they are poorly motivated due
to low salaries. The result is poor access to quality health care and a rapidly developing,
unregulated, private health sector delivering, for a larger part, poor quality care at an
enormous cost to Cambodians. Although nominally free, public health care services still carry
unpredictable informal fees. 75% of health expenditure comes from the people themselves,
with the government supporting only 4% and ODA 21%. This has an impoverishing effect on
the population, and particularly on the poor with 45% having to borrow money to pay for their
health care services.
A significant contribution to the burden of disease is the lack of access to safe drinking water
and sanitation. Despite the abundance of groundwater resources in Cambodia, access to safe
potable water and environmentally sound sanitation facilities in rural and fringe urban areas is
limited. The 1998 General Population Census of Cambodia indicates that 61% of the
population do not have access to safe drinking water and that 86% have no toilet facilities
within their premises.
Objective of UN assistance:
To improve the health and nutritional status of the Cambodian population by assisting
the Government in improving access to quality health services and safe water and by
improving family health and nutrition knowledge and practices

• Better capacities to promote health and prevent and manage health problems at

Component 3.3. Reproductive Health
The reproductive health situation in Cambodia is characterized by high rates of maternal
mortality, a largely unmet need for fertility regulation and a high prevalence of reproductive
tract infections (RTI), sexually transmitted diseases (STD), and HIV/AIDS. Medically trained
personnel assist only 34% of deliveries and about 2,000 Cambodian women die each year of
childbirth-related causes or induced abortions. In 1998, only 21.8% of married women were
using a method of contraception, with only 16.1% using a modern method. HIV/AIDS
prevalence is rising at an alarming rate and its spread is enhanced in the presence of
untreated RTIs and STDs. In addition to its health dimensions, reproductive health conditions
have an impact on overall quality of life and on all aspects of development and therefore need
to be addressed appropriately.

Component 3.4. Education
Although considerable progress has been made since 1979, the education sector in
Cambodia is still facing a number of crises from early childhood to tertiary level which are
characterized by: low net enrolment ratios at pre-school, primary and lower secondary levels
(6%, 78% and 11% respectively), high pupil/teacher ratio, relatively high repetition rate
(particularly during the first years of the primary) and low access to vocational and higher
education. While the enrolment rate for girls is only slightly lower than for boys at the primary
level, the difference increases drastically at secondary and higher levels. The adult literacy
rate is 80% for males and only 57% for females (average rate is 67%). Large proportions of
school age children and illiterate adults are still left outside the education system.
This situation arises from a combination of factors, including protracted armed conflict, low
investment in education (9% of national budget and 1.3% of GDP in 1999), limited
infrastructure, poor quality of facilities, large class sizes, shortages and poor quality of
teaching/learning materials, inadequately trained teachers. Teachers’ salaries are well below
subsistence level, and overall teacher morale is low. The annual population growth rate of 2.4
% poses another burden on the development of the education sector.

status, increased productivity and poverty reduction. Given the present human capital base,
high priority goes to building the capacity at central, provincial and local levels. The UN
system contributions in the education sector will concentrate on: strengthening the capacities
of the Government at all levels concerned to improve the performance of the sector;
improving access to quality basic education (i.e., early childhood, primary and lower

Context and rationale
Environmental issues in Cambodia are high on the agenda of both the Government and the
donor community. This is a reflection of the significant contribution of natural resources to the
national economy as well as the livelihoods of rural households. It is also due to increasing
population and economic pressure on natural resources such as forests and fish. In the
absence of adequate regulations and management frameworks, it is widely assumed that
these pressures will severely degrade the natural resources and the unique ecosystems of
Cambodia. In the medium to long-term, large scale commercial exploitation practices would
also have a negative impact on the economy and the livelihoods of communities currently
benefiting from these resources. The survival of the remaining indigenous cultures could also
be threatened.
The rapid development of a market economy and the opening-up of the country to foreign
interest and investment compound the need to guarantee sustainability in natural resource
management and to ensure equitable allocation of and access to these resources for local
people. The dependency of communities on resources from forests, lakes and protected
areas to ensure their livelihoods calls for development of participatory management
approaches. Issues at stake are equity of access to natural resources as well as the need to
find means of conserving the natural resources while sustaining livelihoods of communities.
In early 1998, the Royal Government of Cambodia adopted the National Environmental Action
Plan (NEAP) which constitutes the Government’s strategy on environmental protection. Its
stated goal is to improve environmental management. The Action Plan provides a strategic
framework to improve environmental management in six priority areas: 1) forest policy, 2)
fisheries and floodplain agriculture in the Tonle Sap region, 3) coastal fisheries, 4) biodiversity and protected areas, 5) energy development and the environment, and 6) urban
waste management. The NEAP states that the common problems in these areas are the
“inadequacy of environmental regulations and the limited institutional capacity and/or political
will to enforce them”. At the February 1999 Consultative Group meeting, the Royal
Government of Cambodia has reiterated its commitment to reforming the management of
natural resources and its commitment to implement a sound forest management scheme (for
which significant preliminary measures have already been taken).
In this context, the UN system will focus its contributions on supporting national efforts in the
following four areas: land use planning, forestry, fisheries, and environmental awareness and
protection. Together, these areas address the main concerns linked with sustainable
management of natural resources in Cambodia. The UN system strategy will be to work for
the preservation and protection of the natural resources and ecosystems of the country while
promoting fair access to natural resource assets for rural and community development.
The UN system in Cambodia, with its experience in working at both the central and
community levels, is uniquely positioned to address issues in this sector. It can, at the same
time, support the development of national natural resource protection policies while promoting
community based development initiatives ensuring that the needs and rights of communities
are respected.
2. Goal of UN System Assistance
To support development and implementation of policies and practices which contribute to
sustainable management of natural resources for local and rural development
Indicators:
• Arable land per capita
• Land area protected
• % of population relying on traditional fuels for energy use
• % change in km2 of forest land in past 10 years
• Forest / woodland as percentage of total landUNDAF CAMBODIA 2001-2005

Component 4.1. Land use
In the present situation of excessive logging, deforestation, land grabbing, uncontrolled
fishing, non-regulated settling, rising demand for agricultural production, etc., there is a very
high risk of over-exploitation and deterioration of natural resources in Cambodia. This
situation calls for the development of land use plans (covering the whole territory, including
forest, lakes and rivers) that will ensure long-term protection and sustainable management of
natural resources while maximizing economic and social benefits to communities and society
as a whole. Such plans would indicate which lands are used for agriculture, which are
reserved for wood product production, fishing grounds, villages and which are fully protected
for bio-diversity conservation.
Objective of UN assistance
Contribute to long-term sustainable management of natural resources through the
development and implementation of integrated land use plans
Development outcomes
• National authorities and local communities have the capacity to prepare and execute a
participatory provincial land use planning exercise
• Land use plans are designed and implemented with the participation of local
communities, NGOs and other stakeholders in representatives areas, contributing to
protection of natural resources and their sustainable use by local communities
Implementation and cooperation modalities
The initial activity of the UN system in the sector will consist of raising awareness in the
Government and ensuring its commitment to the need for participatory land use planning. The
economic potential linked with the improved use of land will be highlighted. The UN system
will advocate for the creation of a land use planning agency at national and provincial level
responsible for the preparation, execution and monitoring of the land use plans and
interacting with all relevant departments. Land use planning should be based on a set of laws
and regulations (land law, fishery laws, forestry laws, investment laws, etc.). The UN system
will support the development, strengthening and implementation of these laws through other
components of the UNDAF (see components 1.1, Legal Framework; 4.2, Forestry; and 4.3,
Fisheries). In return, the preparation of integrated land use plans will directly contribute to the
attainment of the objectives of the Forestry and Fisheries components by developing a
practical tool to manage the forest and fisheries domains.
All activities supported by the UN system organizations for the development of land use plans
(including raising awareness of government officials, building capacities within government
departments and other national institutions (Universities, NGOs, etc.), promoting community
participation in the development and implementation of land use plans, etc.) will be integrated
in a consolidated framework. Its implementation will be supported by different UN
organizations intervening directly or indirectly in the sector, under the leadership of FAO.
A phased approach will be used to design and implement provincial land use plans. Initially,
plans will be developed in a limited number of provinces in which participatory land use
planning is most urgently needed. This could include provinces with a unique set of natural
resources (Ratanakiri, Siem Reap) or with high population pressure (Kampong Cham,
Kandal). Going full-scale would require the mobilization of additional resources from bilateral
and multilateral donors (including the World Bank and IFAD). Linkages between ongoing UN
programmes with experience in community organizations will be strongly promoted.
Cross-cutting issues
The UN system will promote participation of the stakeholders, including women and minority
groups, at all stages of the design of land use plans process. Appropriate consideration will
be given to the specific needs of women and minority groups in terms of access to land and
other natural resources.UNDAF CAMBODIA 2001-2005

Component 4.2. Forestry
Cambodian forests are increasingly at risk with expanding demand for agricultural lands,
timber, and fuel wood due to rapidly increasing population coupled with accelerated economic
development. Current exploitation practices are threatening the livelihoods of communities
living in or around forests plus a perceived decrease in bio-diversity due to habitat
destruction.
Forest degradation and deforestation are driven by economic, social, and political forces,
which are manifested through market, planning and policy failures, population pressures, and
poverty. The RGC’s measures since early 1999 to suppress illegal forest activities and build
a coherent policy have started to yield positive results, however, these measures need to be
consolidated and followed up by appropriate conservation measures.

To strengthen capacities to conserve and manage forest resources and ecosystems while
maximizing the contribution of forestry to employment creation, income generation, rural
development, poverty reduction and economic growth

established with bilateral and multilateral donors (Australia, United Kingdom, World Bank,

Component 4.3. Fisheries
The three fishery sub-sectors (freshwater fisheries, marine fisheries and aquaculture)
contribute significantly to Cambodia’s economy as well as to the livelihoods of its population.
It is for many households a source of income and the primary source of animal protein intake
(70-80%). Primary issues in the sector include: outdated and unenforceable fishery laws, use

of access to fishing grounds for subsistence fishermen, over-fishing, low contribution of
marine fisheries and aquaculture to the national economy and in food security, poor coastal
infrastructure, and illegal fishing in offshore areas and over-fishing of the inshore resources.

as well as the contribution of fisheries to the livelihoods of small-scale fishermen and
communities. It is the intention of the UN system to support national authorities in addressing

2.2. CROSSCUTTING ISSUES
The UN Country Team resolved that the first UNDAF should adopt a crosscutting approach to
address the development challenges of the country. This is being reflected in the choice of areas
of concentration: "Governance, peace and justice", "Poverty reduction", "Human development"
and, to a lesser extent, "Management of natural resources". These are all themes that cut across
many sectors of development as well as across the mandates of specific UN organizations. The
fact that practically all organizations are involved in all of the areas, confirms their crosscutting
and cross mandate nature.
In addition, the UNCT identified seven crosscutting issues that cannot be comprehensively
addressed through any specific component or area of concentration. To be effectively addressed,
these issues need to be in a systematically integrated in many, if not all, of the UNDAF areas and
components. The crosscutting issues are: i) human rights; ii) gender equality and empowerment
of women; iii) minority groups; iv) children and youths’ rights; v) participation and democracy; vi)
regional cooperation; vii) reintegration of demobilized soldiers.
For each of the crosscutting issue identified, this section presents:
i) a short description of the situation regarding this issue;
ii) how the issues are integrated in UN system concerns and plans of action as presented in
Section 2.1.;
iii) which additional activities the UN system will support to address these issues (i.e. activities
that do not fall under the areas of concentration and components presented in section 2.1.);
This sub-section is complemented by section 3.3. presenting how the UN system will go about
addressing these issues in a more coordinated and complementary manner.
i) Human Rights
As stated in the September 1999 Report of the Secretary-General on the situation of human
rights in Cambodia (A/54/353), “some progress has been made, especially in regard to the
recognition of the problems and their true nature. However, some structural problems in the
human rights field still remain”. At the Consultative Group meeting of February 1999, the RGC
reiterated its commitment to strengthen the judiciary, ensure adherence to the rule of law and
promote human rights.
Issues of concern, requiring sustained efforts by the RGC in cooperation with UN organizations,
include the need to strengthen and enhance the competence and independence of the judicial
system, to restore public confidence in it, to tackle the problem of impunity, and to establish the
rule of law. The improvement of prison conditions and the treatment of offenders also warrant
continued attention. While the law-drafting process is continuing, a sound legal framework
providing the structures and safeguards which are necessary to ensure the protection and
promotion of the rights of all still needs to be established. An environment in which civil society
may freely operate, and contribute to the national policy and law making processes, needs to be
preserved. The protection of minorities and the preservation of the culture, livelihood and land
use of the indigenous people are also issues of concern. Ensuring equitable and humane working
conditions for all, preventing and punishing the sexual exploitation of women and children,
ensuring freedom from want and access to quality education and health services remain
important objectives to work towards. It is the intention of the UN system to continue to support
the Government's efforts in the human rights field and to address these problems.
The UN system will promote the rights recognized by the international human rights instruments
through its programmatic activities as well as through advocacy and policy dialogue. These
include the whole range of civil, cultural, economic, political and social rights, including the rights
of women, children, minorities, indigenous people, and other groups requiring special protection.UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005

The objective of the UN system will be to promote the implementation and respect of the
international human rights instruments signed by the Government of Cambodia18. The UN
System will strengthen the Government’s capacities to fulfil its obligations in this regard. It will

Activities of the UN system in that area are in line with the Programme for Reform of the
Secretary-General19. The Programme asserts that “development in the present decade has
underscored that human rights are inherent to the promotion of peace, security, economic

The UN system in Cambodia has endeavored to integrate human rights issues into all its

• promoting the establishment of the rule of law, improving the functioning of the judiciary and

iii) Minority Groups
Minority groups in Cambodia include indigenous people and ethnic minorities. While progress has
been achieved in recognizing their rights and protecting their livelihood, much remains to be done
as stated in the Report of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Human Rights
in Cambodia (E/CN.4/1999/101, 26 February 1999). The cultures, languages and beliefs of the
indigenous communities (highland peoples) are in some respects clearly different from those of
the lowland Khmer and need to be respected and promoted. Their livelihood and subsistence
depend almost entirely on their natural environment, which they use for shifting cultivation and
collecting forest products. However, their customary tenure and access to these natural
resources is not recognized in national or local land-use planning nor in corresponding land rights
and ownership titles. Moreover, the livelihood of highland people is threatened by the current licit
and illicit logging practices as well as by land grabbing practices in or around their area of
residence. Minority groups, and particularly the Vietnamese ethnic minority, are victims of racist
rhetoric and acts of violence. The legal status of ethnic Vietnamese who had lived in Cambodia
for several years needs to be further clarified to ensure their protection.
Through the UNDAF, the UN system will uphold the full enjoyment by indigenous people and
ethnic minorities of their economic, social and cultural rights. Specific activities identified in
section 2.1. that will contribute to this are:
• through its support to the functioning of the judiciary and the drafting of laws, the UN system
will ensure that due consideration is given to protecting the rights of minorities and indigenous
people. (component 1.1.);
• strengthen capacities of NGOs to independently monitor and promote rights of minorities
(1.1.);
• Develop programmes to increase tolerance and mutual understanding towards ethnic
minorities and indigenous peoples as well as respect for cultural diversity (1.3.);
• Promote participation of minority groups in the definition of development interventions at the
local level and their full involvement in the implementation process (2.2.);
• Uphold rights and access of minorities to education and contribute to the development of
languages of minority groups and their use in basic education (3.4.);
• Promote respect for the cultural heritage of indigenous populations (3.4.);
• Promote participation of minority groups in the management at local level of forestry and
fishery resources (4.2. and 4.3.) and in the land planning process (4.1.) as a way to ensure
the sustainability of the interventions and to duly take into account specific situation of
minorities.
In addition, UN system organizations will undertake the following activities that go beyond the
areas of concentration and components presented in section 2.1.:
• as part of its monitoring of possible human rights violations, the COHCHR will continue to

• the United Nations Volunteers (UNV) will continue to support the right to development and the

highland communities in designing and conducting their own development in a manner that
meets their needs and conditions and results in the generation and dissemination of learning
