iv) Children and Youths’ rights
The 1998 census shows that 5.7 million of Cambodians, or approximately 50.5% of the
population, is under 18 years of age. As indicated by UNICEF’s child risk measure, the plight of
Cambodian children is the worst in Asia and one of the worst in the world22. More than half of
children under 5 are malnourished, fewer than 50% are fully immunized, access to basic
education is limited, etc. The number of children in difficult circumstances, including street
children and children victim of exploitation, sexual or other, is increasing.
The UN system will use the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the goals endorsed
at the World Summit for Children23 as the framework for addressing this situation, in cooperation
with the Government. The UN system has an objective to protect and promote children’s rights
and to contribute to the expansion of their opportunities. Through the following components of the
UNDAF, the UN system organizations will work together in improving the living conditions of the
child and youth:
• the rights of the child will be promoted through the rule of law component (1.1.); focus will be
put on the establishment of a legal framework complying with the CRC and a juvenile justice
system as well as on supporting the National Council for Children as the entity promoting
child rights and the implementation of the CRC;
• through the poverty reduction components, the UN system will contribute to the betterment of
the living conditions of the impoverished rural and urban population, including those of
children. Children and youth issues will be fostered through the community development
initiatives;
• through the human development components, particular focus will be put on increasing
access for children to basic education, protecting youth from HIV/AIDS and other STIs,
enhancing access to sexual and reproductive health services for youths, addressing the main
causes of early childhood death (by upgrading quality of primary health care services,
improving coverage of vaccination campaign, etc.), developing specific programmes
addressing educational needs of children in difficult circumstances.
In addition to these, the UN system will undertake the following specific activities:
• UNICEF will give attention to children in particularly difficult circumstances (victims of abuse
and exploitation, children with disabilities, etc.), supporting prevention and early intervention
activities (information, monitoring and referral) at community level and supporting selected
specialized programmes run by both government and non-governmental organizations.
COHCHR will support the legal aspects of these interventions;
• COHCHR and UNICEF will work with the Ministry of Interior and other partners to strengthen
the capacity of law enforcement agents to deal with problem of victims of abuse and sexual
exploitation;
• UNICEF, with the support of the UN system, will advocate for the respect of the rights of the
child to survival, development, protection and participation. The advocacy strategy will be
oriented towards raising public awareness at all levels in government and civil society,
mobilizing political and appropriate financial resource to implement child rights. UNICEF and
ILO will also put emphasis on abolishing the practice of employing children in industries.
• UNICEF and COHCHR will support the Government in fulfilling its obligations under the CRC
and will assist the Cambodian National Council for Children in promoting, monitoring and
reporting on the CRC to the UN Committee, as well as in developing and coordinating policies
and programmes regarding children.

v) Participation and democracy
Participation and democracy are prerequisites for good governance, and little if any of the UN
system’s goals and objectives can be implemented in a meaningful and lasting way without them.
Community involvement, both in the governmental units drafting and implementing development
policies, as well as direct involvement, is crucial for the social cohesion that underlies successful
development. Community participation and stewardship is also the sine qua non for the
sustainable protection of natural and cultural resources.
Cambodia has seen a rapid development of its civil society in the last years and mechanisms are
being tried to allow greater participation of the population at the local level in the decision making
process. Many communities now possess the capacity to plan and manage their own
development. The commune elections (planned for 2001), the creation of commune development
councils and, in parallel, the decentralization process will bring new challenges in terms of
participation.
The objective of the UN system will be to support the development and promotion of participatory
mechanisms that allow the people of Cambodia to participate fully and at all levels in the
development process of the country. Throughout the framework, the UN system will contribute to
foster greater involvement of the population in the activities they are supporting. It will ensure
participation and inclusion of needs of specific groups (women, minority groups, children, exsoldiers, etc.). As indicated in Section 2.1., the UN system will:
• contribute to the establishment of mechanisms to allow representative groups of the society
to be consulted in the elaboration of laws (component 1.1.);
• establish mechanisms to allow greater participation of public and civil society organizations in
decision making processes through its support to the reform of the public administration,
(1.2.);
• in the context of the creation of the commune development councils and the decentralization
process, continue to strengthen the capacities of representatives of communities to
participate into the development planning process local level (2.2.); at the same time, the UN
system will contribute to the definition of participatory mechanisms adapted to the new
administrative structure at the local level (1.2. and 2.2.);
• promote participation of beneficiaries in the management of the education and health
services at local level (2.2., 3.2., 3.4.);
• the UN system will promote participation (of communities, women, minority groups, etc.) in
the management of natural resources area, at all stages of the design and implementation of
land use plans (4.1.) and participation and stewardship in the management of the forestry and
fishery (4.2. and 4.3.).
A participatory political framework (both at the highest and lowest levels of governance) is of
paramount importance for the UN's efforts to be most effective. The UN in the next five years will
focus more on advocating for democracy and participation, leading to increased political trust and
social cohesion. Such a focus will help create a conducive environment for successful
development efforts.
In addition, the UN system will support the commune elections (2001) and the National Assembly
elections (2003), supporting, inter alia, the involvement of civil society organizations in voter
education and election monitoring.
vi) Regional cooperation
With the normalization of Cambodia’s situation and its entry into the Association of Southeast
Asian Nations (ASEAN) in April 1999, Cambodia is increasingly open to the world and to its
neighbors. This brings new opportunities for economic growth and will contribute to strengthening
the economic and political relationship between Cambodia and its neighbors. At the same time,
greater liberalization of movement in goods and people also brings new economic and social
challenges.UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005

In relation to the UNDAF areas of concentration and goals, the main social challenges are a
possible increase in the HIV/AIDS propagation rate; increased human trafficking and increased
exploitation of indigents living in border areas. These aspects will be taken into consideration
when designing programmes addressing HIV/AIDS, supporting the implementation of the legal
framework and poverty reduction respectively. The UN system in Cambodia has already started
the implementation, in collaboration with neighboring countries, of specific programmes
addressing the cross-border aspect of HIV/AIDS and human trafficking.
As a principle, the UN system in Cambodia will endeavor to strengthen regional cooperation and
integration through its programmes. It will implement programmes on a regional basis if this can
contribute to their effectiveness and impact and contribute to strengthen linkages among national
institutions from different countries that can be beneficial to the country and its neighbors.
vii) Reintegration of demobilized soldiers
With the country at peace after years of protracted conflict and the stabilization of the security
situation, the Royal Government of Cambodia has expressed its intention to reform the Royal
Armed Forces of Cambodia and demobilize part of its troops. For the demobilization to be
successful and to contribute to national peace and stability and social cohesion, demobilized
soldiers will need to be rapidly and effectively reintegrated into active civil life. The demobilization
programme would thus include reinsertion and reintegration components.
The programme would be initiated in 2000 with a pilot phase. The international community,
including the UN system, has expressed its intention to support the reintegration stage of the
demobilization. The scale of this programme (up to 40,000 soldiers would be demobilized) and its
impact on community life will require sustained efforts to be efficiently implemented. Financial
commitments from bilateral and multilateral donors are still being sought before going ahead with
the implementation of the programme.
If funding is available, the UN system plans to support the government in successfully
reintegrating demobilized soldiers and their families into local communities, as a means to
support social cohesion, avoid social unrest, and contribute to community development.
Reintegration will be supported mainly through ongoing and planned community development
programmes of UNDP and by programmes supporting the creation of sustainable livelihoods
(agricultural extension programmes, income generating activities, etc.). A specific number of
demobilized soldiers and their families will be designated as beneficiaries of these programmes
once they reintegrate in the areas where these programmes are implemented. In addition, UN
system organizations such as UNICEF will contribute to the development and implementation of
programmes targeted at particular groups, such as children and underage soldiers, as well as the
disabled. In collaboration with the World Bank, specific programmes could also be developed by
ILO to provide demobilized soldiers with employment opportunities through vocational training
and income generating programmes. UNESCO will continue to support literacy and skill training
activities for communities of demobilized soldiers. All programmes would be fully integrated into
local communities, benefiting the entire population.UNDAF Cambodia –2001-2005

Section Three COOPERATION STRATEGIES
UNDAF principles
The UN system organizations participating in the UNDAF will apply a series of principles
when developing and implementing their cooperation programmes in Cambodia. UN system
organizations will:
• define their contributions to the development of the country taking in full consideration the
priorities established by the Government;
• support the attainment of the development goals emanating from UN global conferences;
• promote national ownership of programmes and projects and ensure their sustainability;
• favor national execution and use of the SWAp and programme approach;
• mainstream human rights into their programmes and promote full respect of all human
rights, including the right to development and social, economic and cultural rights;
• mainstream gender issues and promote gender equality through their programmes and
projects;
• support the development of national and regional partnerships;
• encourage full participation of beneficiaries in programme formulation and
implementation;
• contribute to the sustainable development of national capacities;
• encourage partnership and coordination among all development partners and;
• support the development and strengthening of an active civil society and its involvement
in national affairs.
3.1. IMPLEMENTATION MODALITIES
The goals and objectives of the UNDAF will be addressed by UN system organizations by
providing assistance for capacity development, promoting national execution, increasingly
targeting its assistance and by promoting the use of SWAp and the programme approach.
Capacity development and delivery of services
The type of assistance provided by the UN system to Cambodia has gradually shifted over
the past years as the country was moving from a conflict to a post-conflict situation. While
provision of direct support for the delivery of services to the population has been reduced,
more emphasis has been gradually put on building or strengthening the capacities and skills
of national institutions and local organizations to efficiently develop and implement policies
and programmes which support the development process of the country.
Capacity development will continue to be the main thrust of UN system assistance to
Cambodia. Both the RGC and the UN system recognized that significant programmes of
reform have to be implemented or consolidated in the four areas of concentration covered by
the UNDAF. The capacities of the institutions and organizations mandated to develop and
implement these reforms at the central and local level still need to be consolidated to ensure
their success. As indicated in Section One, the UN system has both the experience and the
capacity to play a vital role in strengthening the capacity of national institutions to efficiently
and effectively address these challenges.
The attainment of the goals, objectives and development outcomes presented in Section Two
will require that capacity development efforts be targeted at public institutions both at the
central and local levels. The capacity of civil society organizations and local NGOs to
effectively contribute to the development process of the country by identifying and
implementing programmes and advocating for priority issues will also be strengthened. In the
wake of the planned establishment of elected commune councils with the authority to plan
and manage local development, the UN system will make particular efforts to strengthen the
capacities of institutions and organizations at the village and commune level.
Promoting national ownership and ensuring sustainability of the institutions benefiting from
capacity development assistance will continue to be a priority. Favoring national execution
and designing programmes in collaboration with national authorities and that respond toUNDAF Cambodia –2001-2005

Government priorities will contribute to national ownership. The ongoing reform of the public
administration (supported by the UN system) should improve the performance of Cambodia's
administration and ensure a greater retention rate of civil servants benefiting from the UN
system capacity development programmes, thus contributing to sustainability of UN
supported programmes.
The UN system is disposed to promote and engage in a broad-based dialogue with national
authorities and the development community on capacity development and the use of external
technical assistance. This dialogue will be conducted with a view to harmonize procedures,
improve efficiency and effectiveness and ensure sustainability of these types of assistance.
During the first UNDAF cycle, the UN system will continue supporting the provision of social

increasingly targeted to specific vulnerable groups and regions. As the country develops and
public spending in social sectors increases, the needs of the entire population will be
increasingly met through national resources, this kind of assistance should gradually

National Execution
UN system organizations have a long and varied experience in working inside government
structures. Past experience, particularly in the health and community development sectors,
have indicated that national execution, while ensuring national ownership, can increase the
impact of UN system supported activities. The UN system will continue to work inside
government structures and to promote national execution of UN system projects and
programmes when feasible. If necessary, appropriate technical and managerial support will
be provided to national institutions entrusted with the responsibility of implementing or
executing projects or programmes. Increasing use of national execution modality will not
preclude the provision of services by specialized agencies who will continue to contribute
technical assistance to support the implementation of projects and programmes.
UN system organizations supporting the same institutions at the central and local level will
endeavor to avoid duplication of management structures. By pooling their human and physical
resources together they will benefit from economy of scale while also reducing the burden on
national counterparts.
The UN system will increase the use of national NGOs and civil society organizations as
implementing agents in line with gradual disengagement of the government from running the
economy, and with the development of a vibrant civil society. Paralleling this, the UN system
will increase capacity building efforts targeted at these organizations to increase their
capabilities to become efficient development partners. When working with NGOs and CSOs,
the UN system will endeavor to ensure that they relate to the Government structures and
policies. The UN system will also work increasingly with the private sector.
Targeting
To increase the impact of its assistance and to make a significant contribution to poverty
reduction and human development, the UN system will endeavor to increasingly target its
resources to the most vulnerable groups and to the poorer areas of the country (see area of
concentration two: Poverty Reduction). Objective criteria will be used to identify provinces,
communes and districts where poverty is highest and with the lowest level of human
development. Taking into consideration Government programmes and assistance provided by
other partners, the UN system will identify vulnerable groups as well as rural and urban areas
where their assistance should be increasingly targeted.
The UNDAF Monitoring Working Group will supervise the identification of vulnerability and of
the poorest areas and will monitor allocation of resources of UN system organizations to
ensure that the objectives of targeting assistance are met.UNDAF Cambodia –2001-2005

Sector wide approach24 and programme approach
During the UNDAF cycle, the UN system will support the use of sector wide approach and
programme approach as a way to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of external aid and
strengthen local capacities in a coordinated and cohesive manner.
The RGC is contemplating leading the SWAp process in several sectors, starting with the
health sector. Later on, the Government may develop SWAp for the following sectors:
education, rural infrastructure, governance, and private sector development / financial sector
development. The preparation of a SWAp for the health sector has already been initiated by
the Government with the support of WHO.
In all sectors where SWAps may be developed, the UN system will support the Government in
assuming full ownership of the process and play the lead role in implementing the sector wide
approach. Its involvement will also be based on a genuine interest from external partners
involved in the sector, to participate in the process. The UN system organizations involved in
the sectors will define their contribution to the preparation and implementation of the SWAps
in a coordinated way using the UNDAF as a frame of reference.
The UN system could make specific contribution in developing a SWAp by: i) supporting the
involvement of all partners (donors and local organizations); ii) building the capacity of the
government to manage and implement the process; iii) facilitating the pooling of resources
and harmonization of procedures that would be necessary for the implementation of the
SWAps.
By supporting the development and implementation of SWAps, the UN system will endeavor
to ensure that they contribute to the attainment of the four goals of the UNDAF regarding
governance, peace and justice, poverty reduction, human development and sustainable
management of natural resources. It will also ensure that proper attention is given to
crosscutting issues such as human rights and gender equality.

Section Four IMPLEMENTATION, FOLLOW-UP AND REVIEW
Provisions for follow-up and review of the UNDAF are based on the principle that the UNDAF is a
living document. It is a framework to guide the contributions of the UN system organizations to
the development process of the country during the next five years (2001-2005). As development
is a process, however, the UNDAF must adapt itself to respond to changes in the country
situation. The UNDAF will thus be regularly reviewed and, if necessary, reoriented to respond to
the best of the UN system’s ability to meet the needs of the country.
4.1. IMPLEMENTATION
4.1.1. Country cooperation programmes
The provisions of the UNDAF will be implemented through country cooperation programmes
agreed to by participating organizations and the Royal Government of Cambodia. The selection
and definition of goals, objectives and intervention strategies, as well as the pattern of resource
allocation in the programmes and projects of individual organizations, will be consistent with the
UNDAF. The individual country programme and project documents will specify how they are
contributing to the achievement of the UNDAF objectives. It is the responsibility of individual
organizations and of the UN system as a whole, to ensure that the provisions of the UNDAF are
reflected in these programmes.
The individual country cooperation programmes of UN system organizations usually vary in
duration and type. In Cambodia, the four "funding organizations" of the United Nations
Development Group, (UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF and WFP) agreed in 1998 to harmonize their
programme cycle from 2001 onward. The country cooperation programme of these organizations
will thus follow the duration of the UNDAF cycle (2001-2005)25. The programmes will be finalized
in 2000 and endorsed by the Royal Government of Cambodia and the Executive Boards of the
specific organizations.
The UN technical organizations (i.e. COHCHR, UNESCO, UNHCR, FAO, UNAIDS and WHO)
follow different programming modalities. By legislation, these organizations do not have a country
cooperation programme, as the funding organizations do. Nevertheless, these organizations have
committed themselves, through the UNDAF, to align, when possible and relevant, their
programmes and projects with the duration of the UNDAF. Harmonization of programme cycles is
considered a key element of the UNDAF. It will facilitate the process of joint assessment and joint
programming and should also reduce the burden imposed on Government entities to participate
in parallel programming processes.

Inter-agency Coordination Tools
The UN system will use the following tools to facilitate the joint monitoring of the implementation
of the provisions of the UNDAF: the UNDAF annual workplan; the CCA indicator framework;
thematic and sector reviews; the new CCA.
The UN system will develop at the end of each year (from 2000 to 2004) an annual UNDAF
workplan. Using the UNDAF document as a reference as well as the latest policy orientation of
the government, the workplan will identify precise benchmark indicators giving clear indication of
the specific outputs and outcomes expected in the coming year for each of the UNDAF
components. The workplan should cover programmatic as well as non-programmatic activities
(e.g. advocacy, partnership building, public information).
At the end of the year, the workplan will be used to prepare the annual review of the UNDAF (see
section 4.3.). In turn, the following year workplan will be prepared by taking into consideration the
findings of the annual review completed for the year before. If necessary, the workplan will reflect
the need to reorient the UNDAF objectives and development outcomes for each component as
well as the approach followed to attain these objectives and outcomes.
The UNDAF workplan will be prepared under the guidance of the UNDAF Monitoring Working
Group and submitted to the UNCT to be reviewed and endorsed at their annual retreat. It will be
shared with the Government and other concerned partners and be used to strengthen
partnerships with donors as it will endeavor to define what their contribution to the UNDAF will be.
The workplan will therefore guide the work of participating organizations for the year to come and
facilitate the monitoring of progress made in achieving the goals and objectives of the UNDAF.
Joint thematic or sector review could eventually be undertaken by all organizations involved in
one sector. These reviews could, for example, be undertaken in the context of the preparation of
a SWAp for a sector and would contribute to the definition of the support that could be given by
the UN system to that particular sector. The UNCT and the UNDAF Monitoring working group will
examine the opportunity of undertaking such reviews in collaboration with the Government and
other partners.
The Common Country Assessment Indicator Framework (see Annex A) will be updated as
reliable new data on the demographic, social, economic and governance situation becomes
available. The indicator framework will be used as a reference for monitoring the development
situation and reporting on progress made in achieving the international conferences goals. The
use of the indicator framework by all UN system organizations will ensure consistency in reporting
on the situation of the country.
The UN system will produce a new Common Country Assessment in the first semester of 2004,
as a first step for the preparation of the second UNDAF for Cambodia (to be initiated in 2006).
The new CCA will be prepared in a participatory manner involving the UN system and its
partners. It will represent the position of the UN system on the development challenges of the
country, based on the goals and recommendations emanating from the international conferences.

4.3. REVIEW AND EVALUATION MODALITIES
Monitoring and evaluation of the UNDAF is the responsibility of the UN system organizations
participating in the UNDAF. As the provisions of the UNDAF are implemented through
participating UN system organizations’ programmes and projects, these organizations have the
responsibility to monitor the day-to-day implementation of the provision of the framework. On a
macro-level, the UNDAF will need to be reviewed and evaluated by the UN system to ensure that
it remains relevant to national development needs and priorities and continues to be an effective
tool for enhancing UN system collaboration. The UN system will monitor and evaluate the UNDAF
in close partnership with the Government.
The UNDAF for Cambodia will be reviewed annually, at mid-term and at the end of the UNDAF
cycle. In a general manner, the annual review, the mid-term review and the end of cycle
evaluation will each address the following three main set of issues:
- the management of the process, i.e. the efficiency of collaboration in implementing the
provisions of the UNDAF within the UN system;
- the results, i.e. the specific achievements of the UNDAF in terms of meeting the objectives
and development outcomes identified in section 2;
- the outcomes, i.e. the differences made by working under a joint framework.
The review process will also include a review of how the crosscutting issues have been integrated
and addressed. It will examine the UNDAF’s contribution to the attainment of conference
outcomes and what progress has been made on the two UN “corporate” priority: halving absolute
poverty and the girls’ education initiative.
Annual Review
The annual review will be undertaken by the UNDAF monitoring working group using local
resources. It will be a light exercise that will review progress achieved so far and investigate ways
to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the UNDAF provisions and modalities. The annual
review will be based on the findings of the annual review of country programmes or projects
conducted by participating organizations, focusing on their contribution to meeting UNDAF
objectives. The annual review will be shared with the partners of the UN system. The results of
the annual review of the UNDAF will feed in the Annual Report of the Resident Coordinator
covering progress made in implementing the provisions of the UNDAF.
Mid-term Review
The mid-term review will be undertaken in the second semester of 2003 with the participation of
the Government, donors and other development partners. The review will assess how the goals
and objectives of the UNDAF have been achieved so far, the contribution of individual
organization programmes to achieve these goals as well as the impact of the UNDAF on
coordination of the overall UN system activities to meet development objectives. The review
could, if necessary, lead to a reorientation of the UNDAF goals and objectives to bring them in
line with progress made so far and with the new development situation and the new Government
priorities.
The review will be undertaken with the support of consultants external to the UN system, and be
organized and monitored by the UNDAF Monitoring Working Group in collaboration with the
Royal Government of Cambodia. The UNDAF mid-term review will respond to the need to review
the country programmes of UNDP, UNFPA and UNICEF. The modalities of the review will be
worked out to meet the specific requirements of all organizations participating in the UNDAF.UNDAF Cambodia 2001-2005

Monitoring the implementation of the provisions of the UNDAF with the Government
As indicated above, the Government will be closely involved in reviewing the implementation of
the provisions of the UNDAF. The following mechanisms will be used for this purpose:
- the UNDAF annual review will be shared with the Government and the annual workplan be
prepared in consultation with the Government to ensure that priorities identified by the

- the Government will officially be part of the team that will review the UNDAF at mid-term.

activities supported by the UN system in a comprehensive manner. These meetings should take
place under the aegis of the Cambodian Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Board. The meetings
will be used to foster policy dialogue on development priorities and to address the main issues
which arise from the implementation of the provisions of the UNDAF.
4.4. RESOURCE MOBILIZATION
As indicated, the UNDAF will be implemented through individual country programmes and
projects the UN system organizations. Therefore the larger part of the resources necessary to
implement the provisions of the UNDAF will come from the core and non-core funds of
participating organizations. In addition to the funds they receive from their headquarters, all UN
system organizations in Cambodia are mobilizing non-core resources from bilateral and
multilateral donors. During the UNDAF cycle, UN system organizations will continue to mobilize
resources for their programmes and will remain fully accountable to donors on the use of these
resources.
Increasingly, donor contributions to the core budget of UN system organizations are diminishing,
while contributions to specific programmes with clearly defined outcomes and / or contributions to
specific countries are increasing. This challenges the UN system organizations to develop high
quality programmes at the field level and at the same time build strong partnerships with bilateral
and multilateral donors based on common or convergent interests. By supporting the Programme
of Reform of the United Nations, the donor community is also expecting the UN system
organizations to present a clear and coherent picture of their funding requirements at the field
level.
In that general context, the UNDAF will be used to facilitate resource mobilization by presenting
to the donor community a comprehensive and coherent picture of the activities the UN agencies
are going to be involved in, in the years to come, as well as the funding requirements to
implement these activities. Joint efforts at resource mobilization will focus on areas where the
gaps in funding are more important (section 5) as well as on joint programmes and projects to be
developed and implemented in the framework of the UNDAF. For accountability reasons,
resources will continue to be mobilized and managed on an agency-by-agency basis.UNDAF Cambodia 2001-2005

4.5. UNDAF AND AID COORDINATION
The UN system recognizes that, in Cambodia like elsewhere, the responsibility of external aid
coordination rests primarily with the host Government. The aid coordination process and
mechanisms used in Cambodia are briefly described in Annex B, "Status of development
cooperation in the country". The UN system in Cambodia will continue to support these
mechanisms.
The regular meetings of the Consultative Group are the principal mechanism by which the
Government and its development partners exchange on the priorities of the country. These
meetings provide an opportunity for the Government to present and discuss its development
priorities and the actions it intends to take to address these priorities with the donor community.
The Government also indicates at the meetings its external funding requirements for the coming
three years. The Consultative Group meetings have been followed since 1999 by quarterly incountry meetings. Through those meetings, the Government and donors exchange information
and views on the progress made in implementing agreed upon reforms. Four consultative donor
groups have been established to facilitate the review process in the areas of fiscal reform,
demobilization, public administration reform, forestry and social sectors. The last three donor
groups are currently chaired by UNDP, FAO and UNICEF respectively.
During the UNDAF period, the UN system will continue to support the Consultative Group
process. It intends to: i) provide technical support to the Government to prepare the
documentation for the meetings upon request, and to implement the recommendations of the
meetings; ii) continue playing a facilitator role in the in-country follow-up process to the CG
meetings. The UN system will also advocate an enlargement of the functions of the donor
consultative groups. These groups should not only facilitate donor preparation to the upcoming
quarterly and yearly meetings, but also contribute to enhancing coordination among donors in
programme development and implementation.
The UN system will also contribute to aid coordination by continuing to play a facilitating role
among donors in supporting the Government as it defines its priorities in certain areas of
development and presents these in a comprehensive manner to the donor community. At the
request of the government, such type of support could be provided for the health sector, the
reform of public administration, mine action, the support to the electoral process, the reform of the
judiciary and the decentralization process.UNDAF Cambodia 2001-2005

Annex A COMMON COUNTRY ASSESSMENT INDICATOR FRAMEWORK
The Indicator Framework presented here is an instrument prepared initially to assist the United
Nations Country Team in the preparation of the CCA. Over the long term, it can also contribute to
the monitoring of the implementation of the provisions of the UNDAF. Its main purpose is to
highlight potential major issues in a country by focusing attention on and measuring progress in
specific areas. The list of indicators contained in this annex, while limited, represents an attempt
to reflect a balanced representation of key issues and provide a means of entry into the areas
covered by the mandates of UN system organizations. Indicators included in the list are based
on the list provided in the CCA Guidelines (April 1999, New York). A limited number of indicators
have been added to reflect the specificity of the Cambodian situation.
The CCA Indicator Framework comprises three components:
a) First, indicators relating to development goals and objectives set forth in UN conventions,
conferences and declarations in the area of poverty eradication, health, gender, education,
etc (page 85). This group of indicators builds upon the existing established global lists of
OECD, the World Bank and the UN, the ACC document on Basic Social Services for All and
the Minimum National Social Data Set;
b) Second, basic contextual indicators relating to the demographic and economic conditions of a
country, which provide the necessary background for understanding development concerns
(page 91);
c) Third, information on the status of legal provisions related to international human rights
instruments and political and civil rights (page 93).
The three main criteria that guided the selection of the indicators were as follows:
a) Indicators should provide relevant and robust measures of progress towards goals and
objectives contained in UN conventions, conferences and declarations; they should be clear
and relatively straightforward to interpret; and they should provide a basis for international
comparison;
b) Indicators should not impose an unnecessary burden on countries and where practicable
should be broadly consistent with other global lists;
c) Insofar as possible, the indicators should be constructed from existing and well-established
data sources, be quantifiable and capable of consistency of measurement over time.
The CCA indicators can be used as measures of progress along a large numbers of development
concerns. It follows that, in an ideal situation, the indicators are needed for at least two points in
time. Or preferably time trends of 5 to 10 years intervals. This would enable changes in the level
or quality of development progress to be measured through changes in the values of the
indicators.
Unfortunately, the scarcity of reliable data in Cambodia prior to the mid-1990 prevents for the time
being to, for most of the indicators, present time trends. This obstacle should be overcome
gradually in the years to come as Cambodia is building up its data collection capacity and
undertake surveys using robust methodology on a regular basis. In the meantime, surveys
undertaken in the past years might have used different modalities and produced results that are
not always readily comparable. This might explains why, for example, data collected through the
1998 General Census and through the 1997 Socio-Economic Survey might differs. Data collected
through these surveys have nevertheless been put together in the CCA indicator framework in
order to provide an overview of the situation for each indicators. Each data collection exercise
can be consulted to obtain more complete information about the nature of the survey, its
coverage and limitations.
Decision was made to rely mainly on first-hand information and thus to only present data
collected in-country and not data extrapolated from previous data collection exercise. The flip side
of this approach is that data presented here may appear outdated or incomplete compare to data UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005

Annex B LESSONS LEARNED
• While its true that the challenges facing Cambodia are formidable, it is important to
remember that many of the problems are interconnected. Clearly, a holistic approach to
development assistance that recognizes the linkages between social spending and
poverty, environmental degradation and population growth, and child schooling, health
and nutrition, will have much greater effect than piece-meal efforts to address each
problem individually.
• The fiscal reform as well as reform of the public administration holds the key to the
sustainability of development projects and programmes. Without such a reform, donor
interventions will continue to be restrained in their impact.
• Co-ordination is easier and more effective where national programmes exist. Such
programmes enable donors to integrate their inputs into a goal-related, elaborated
framework and to track progress – financial and substantive – using single reporting and
evaluation mechanisms. Separate accounting and reporting by and for each donor is
inefficient, and places impossible demands on government counterparts.
• Close consultations between UN agencies need to take place at the project/programme
conceptualization and planning phases, in order to fully exploit each agency's
comparative advantages. To achieve programmatic synergy, the UN system will also
have to interact closely with bilateral agencies.
• Wide divergences remain in the degree of decentralization and delegation accorded by
different UN agencies. Several specialized agencies are obliged to refer relatively minor
policy and financial issues to their regional/global headquarters for decision. Such
differences in administrative regulations and practices limits the value-added of UN
system co-operation.
• Post-project financial sustainability is vital for the lasting impact of development project
and programmes. No donor should be allowed to ignore this, or to shuffle responsibility on to
someone else (usually "the government"). At the micro level, every project should contain
specific short-term, post-project, coping proposals (cost recovery, bridging funds, etc.), linked
to urgent action at the macro level.
• Facing weak institutional capacities and delivery requirement, the tendency to provide
substitution assistance can be strong. Efforts to effectively develop or strengthen national
capacities must be reinforced and constant.
• UN system organizations must have the capacity to adapt its support to face emerging
priorities as the country is going through prolonged period of peace and stability and
enjoyed sustained economic growth. With the liberalization of the economy and the
political situation. Flexibility must also be shown to be able to adapt programmes to the
foreseen diminution of resources allocated to Cambodia and to UN organizations by
bilateral and multilateral partners. Modalities to address this challenge should be sought.
• Systematic inter-agency collaboration and team building should not only take place at the
level of Heads of Agencies but at all level of personnel. Improved information sharing
mechanisms and exchange of best practices would contribute to greater efficiency and
increased impact of UN system activities.UNDAF Cambodia - 2001-2005 99

Annex C Overview of Official Development Assistance
Introduction1
Cambodia remains heavily dependent on external financial and technical assistance. During 1992-1998,
Cambodia received some US$ 2,7 billion in Official Development Assistance (ODA), i.e. around US$ 390
million on average per year. This roughly corresponds to an average of US$ 34 per capita per year. In 1998,
the value of ODA represented 70% of domestic exports and 167% of Government revenue.
Registered pledges by donor countries and organizations have averaged at about US$ 500 million per year
since 1992. The difference between the level of pledges and disbursement can be explained by the internal
political and economical situation as well as by the donor procedures causing delays in turning pledges into
disbursements. Despite the high level of pledges and disbursements, the relationship between the
government and the international donor community has not always been easy-going. As a direct
consequence of the deterioration of the political situation in the country in mid-1997, total donor
disbursement decreased from US$ 520 million in 1996 to US$ 375 million in 1997. This reduction was
directly related to the suspension of aid by some donors, notably the United States and Germany
(subsequently restored). Other countries took up a wait-and-see attitude - in most cases maintained
throughout the national elections in mid-1998 - resulting in long delays in the implementation of many
development programs and projects. Non-definitive figures for 1999 indicate that ODA disbursement was
roughly at the same level as in 1998.
The political turmoil of 1997 and 1998 and its effects has complicated analysis of ODA trends in Cambodia.
The expected increase in 1999 in the level of ODA disbursement following the positive outcome of the CG
meeting of February has yet to materialize, partly because of delays in initiating new projects. Some donors
have also remained cautious as they expect clear signs from the Government that it will live-up to the
commitments made at the meeting. In addition to this, because of the decline in ODA globally and the fact
that Cambodia is no longer a priority country for many donors, it is unlikely that the level of external
assistance to be received in the future will reach the level of 1995-96 (i.e. more than $500 million/year). This
trend could be counterbalanced, however following the partial resumption of balance of payment and
budgetary support assistance. Already, the IMF has resumed its balance of payment assistance and the
World Bank could approve a structural adjustment credit in the second quarter of 2000.

The 1992-1998 ODA disbursement figures show there is no doubt in the increasing importance of technical
assistance in relation to other types of external assistance (investment project assistance, budgetary and
balance-of-payment support, food aid, and emergency and relief assistance). Another observation is that,
although an increasing proportion of external assistance takes the form of loans rather than grants, freestanding and investment-related technical assistance is still almost entirely grant funded. A detailed
analysis of ODA trends and distribution is given below.
Sectoral distribution of ODA
In Cambodia, the five largest recipient sectors of ODA are area/rural development (14 percent of total during
the period 1992-1998), development administration (12 percent), transport/ infrastructure (12 percent),
economic management (11 percent), and humanitarian/relief aid (11 percent).
Area/rural development
With the establishment of an integrated rural development structure at the provincial, district, commune or
village levels, the Government is effecting a decentralized approach to rural development planning, financing
and implementation. Provincial capacity building efforts are being supported by technical assistance
financed by ODA, including through UNDP and UNICEF. In addition, rural credit programmes and grassroots oriented production programmes are being supported by local and international NGOs. In 1995, the
Social Fund started operations, with initial assistance from the World Bank to generate rural employment
and to support the restoration of essential rural infrastructure through quick, small-scale rehabilitation and
reconstruction efforts identified and implemented by the communities themselves. Demining is another area
that has received significant ODA resources during the last five years, resulting in an effective demining and
un-exploded ordnance clearance capacity for the country.
Scarcity of entrepreneurial skills and lack of access to credit are two of the major stumbling blocks to rural
development and economic self-sufficiency in Cambodia. In response to this situation, vocational skills
training as well as financial services to micro and small business entrepreneurs are being provided by a
number of local and international NGOs, often with the backing of bilateral and multilateral donors.
Development administration and economic management
The inadequate functioning of the Cambodian state apparatus and the low level of domestic revenues cast
doubts on the government's financial and technical capabilities to retain the skills and institutional
structures created with the help of donor support. At the same time, capacity building components of
projects have been given more priority and prominence.
Practically all Cambodian ministries involved in overall economic planning and management receive some
sort of external assistance to strengthen institutional structures and develop human resources. In addition,
donors have supported independent research and training institutions in their efforts to strengthen individual
skills in economic analysis and are increasingly supporting civil society organizations.

Transport/infrastructure
Investments in the infrastructure and transport sector have mainly been realized through loans and technical
assistance grants provided by the World Bank, ADB and the European Union (EU) as well as by bilateral
donors such as Japan, France, Germany, China, Denmark and Sweden. UNDP, WFP and ILO are also
providing support in that area. The support has been targeted to the rehabilitation of the primary roads
network, rural roads, bridges and ferry crossings with a view to facilitate transport of freight, agricultural
produce and the integration of markets.
In 1998, an estimated 500 km of roads was reconstructed, and another 550 km rehabilitated. Most of the
main road arteries, including many urban, provincial and rural roads, have been improved by resurfacing or
widening, as well as by the rebuilding of bridges and culverts. Secondary and tertiary roads have been
strengthened, particularly in the north and north-western provinces, with new roads being built under
targeted rural development programmes. In addition, railway tracks, bridges and culverts are progressively
being rehabilitated, with locomotives, rolling stock and wagon repairand renovation workshops.
Nevertheless, substantial investments of at least US$ 1 billion will still be required over the next five years to
improve road, water and rail transport, irrigation, water supply and sanitation, as well as electricity
distribution and power generation services.
Humanitarian aid/relief and social sectors
After three decades of civil strife and conflict, it should be no surprise that the Humanitarian Aid/Relief
sector accounts for more than a tenth (11 percent) of total ODA disbursed 1992-98. However, as preconditions for long term development improved during the 1990s, this type of assistance has gradually
declined - by about 25 percent annually since 1992. The main players in this sector have been local and
international NGOs, UN agencies (particularly WFP and UNHCR) and bilateral donors including Canada,
France, Belgium, Japan, Sweden, UK, and the Netherlands.
Social Sectors
While the proportion of ODA allocated to the "social" sectors has been increasing, it is still quite low
compared to regional averages. Combined education/human resource development, health and social
development (including sanitation, safe water and culture) received about 23 percent of total disbursements
during 1992-1998. A more detailed analysis of disbursements in the social sectors would probably show
that globally donors have allocated less then 20 percent of their assistance to basic social services, thus
failing to meet the international target endorsed in the Copenhagen Social Summit and know as the "20/20
initiative".
Geographical distribution of ODA
Increased allocation of ODA and other budgetary resources to the rural areas is widely accepted by the
government and the international donor community as a prerequisite for sustained poverty reduction in
Cambodia. Nevertheless, some donors still have a strong preference for providing assistance to Phnom
Penh and/or to central institutions rather than to some of the more isolated and impoverished regions on the
country.
According to the Development Cooperation Report 1998/19992, 60 percent of total ODA provided 1994-1998
has been spent on what is described as countrywide programmes. For the same period, about 25 percent
was allocated to the Phnom Penh area and only around 19 percent was specifically earmarked for other
provinces. Among these, Kompong Speu (3 percent), Siem Reap (2 percent), Battambang (2 percent) and
Takeo (2 percent) were the largest recipients. Kandal, Kampong Cham, Prey Veng, Bantey Meanchey,
Svay Rieng and Kampot all received about 1 percent each of total ODA for the same period.
While available data indicates than an increasing share of ODA has been allocated to provinces other than
Phnom Penh in the past five years (from 16 percent in 1994 to 19 percent in 1998), greater efforts by both
governments and donors are needed to further increase the share of ODA directed towards rural areas,
where 85 percent of the population and 90 percent of the country's poor live.

ODA disbursements by type and terms
Of the total amount of ODA disbursed 1992-98, free-standing technical co-operation accounted for US$ 970
million (35 percent), investment-related technical co-operation for US$ 171 million (6 percent), investment
project assistance for US$ 852 million (31 percent), budgetary aid and balance of payments support for US$
291 million (11 percent), food aid for US$ 82 million (3 percent), and emergency relief assistance for US$
387 million (14 percent). Over the same period, the disbursement of grants for all types of development
assistance totaled US$ 2.3 billion, while loans amounted to US$ 435 million.
Free-standing and investment-related technical cooperation
The period 1992-1998 sawa clear trend in the increasing importance of free-standing and investment-related
technical cooperation in relation to other types of external assistance. From around 19 per cent of the total
in 1992, the share of these two types of ODA rose to 40 per cent in 1995 and around 57 percent in 1998.
This is a trend that some within the government find worrying, doubting its effectiveness and knowledge of
the state of the country's physical infrastructure. This trend could be reversed in 2000 following the
signature in recent months of accords for the funding of investment type projects.
Although an increasing proportion of external assistance takes the form of loans rather than grants, freestanding and investment-related technical assistance is still almost entirely grant-funded. This is also an
area of concern for the government, which tries to restrict the proportion of expenditure on technical
assistance in loan-funded projects to 20 per cent or below.
Another fairly clear trend is an increase in the importance of multilateral relative to bilateral donors in the
provision of free-standing and investment-related technical cooperation. Multilaterals (UN system agencies,
ADB, EU and the World Bank) accounted for less than a third of such expenditure in 1992 but almost half in
1997. Although accurate figures are not available, free-standing and investment-related technical
cooperation funded by NGOs has almost certainly also been growing in relative importance: in contrast to
the other categories of donors, their total external assistance continues to grow strongly.
Investment project assistance
Investment project assistance - cash or in kind contribution to specific capital investment projects - has
increased as a share of total ODA at an annual average rate of 21 percent since 1992. The majority of the
funds allocated to this purpose originates in multilateral institutions such as the ADB, EU, and the World
Bank, as well as in bilateral donors, including Japan, China, France, Germany, Netherlands, Sweden, UK
and the United States.
The government’s Public Investment Program (PIP) forecasts that an average minimum of US$ 350 million
per year in this category would be required for the next three years to rehabilitatedevastated infrastructure
and to respond to the huge needs in the social sectors, in particular in health and education. The promotion
of private investments in transport, power generation, telecommunications, etc. will be of vital importance in
this respect.

Budgetary aid/balance of payments support
During the period 1992-1998, the Cambodian government sawan average annual decrease of 34 percent in
budgetary aid/balance of payments support form donors. The negative trend culminated in 1997-1998, when
no loan funds for either budget or balance of payments support were released by international financial
institutions due to the government's lack of commitment to economic reforms. 1999 saw this situation put
to an end with the resumption of IMF lending operations.
According to the PIP, a minimum of US$ 50 million of budgetary support are required for the years 1999-
2001 to avoid potential shortfalls that may in turn lead to reduced spending on economic sectors as well as
social services. Continued support under this category would also be needed as a cushion for coming
interest payments on loans.
Food aid/emergency and relief assistance
Food aid/emergency and relief assistance have declined at an average annual rate of 13 percent since 1992
as a share of the total ODA. While this type of assistance represented 51 and 22 percent of total ODA in
1992 and 1993 respectively, it only represented 3 percent in 1998. Funds under this category have mainly
been provided by international NGOs, UN system agencies and from bilaterals such as Canada, France,
Belgium, Japan, Netherlands, Sweden, and the UK.
ODA Disbursements by Donors
Following the complex operations of UNTAC and the repatriation of Cambodians from Thailand supported by
WFP and UNHCR, the UN system continues to play a prominent role in the development of Cambodia.
With poverty eradication as a principal, common focus, UN agencies are providing substantial support in a
number of areas ranging from macro-economic management, health and education sector reform, natural
resource management, participatory rural development to good governance and human rights. During the
period 1992-1998, collectively, the UN system organizations delivered some US$ 236 million from their own
resources plus roughly US$ 412 million from other donors’ funds entrusted to them. The relative importance
of ODA provided by the UN system, in percentage of the total disbursement of ODA, has remained relatively
stable in the last years, hovering around 10-11%.Bilateral donors have continued to use the UN System
organizations to channel around 25% of their collective ODA to Cambodia.

Other major multilateral donors include the EU, World Bank, ADB and the IMF. These institutions delivered
a combined total of US$ 616 million during the period 1992-1998, mainly for purposes such as the quick
rehabilitation of infrastructure, sound macro-economic management, power and water supply improvement,
rural development, environmental protection and promotion, basic education and health and national aid
coordination.
Bilateral donors collectively provided about US$ 1.8 billion or 64 percent of total ODA 1992-1998. According
to the DCR 1998/1999, the largest bilateral donors - in order of financial contributions - for the same period
were Japan, France, the United States, Australia, Sweden, the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, China,
the United Kingdom and Canada. Quite a few of these donors channel their support, either in part or
entirely, through UN system agencies and/or through NGOs.3 Thus, many bilateral donors share the
objectives and priorities of the multilateral donors exemplified above.
NGOs provided a total of US$ 187 million in “core or own” resources (including funds from private donors,
religious bodies, philantrophic organizations and other non-government funding bodies) to Cambodia during
1992-1998. Their activities cover a wide range of areas, including health, area/rural development, social and
community development, and education/vocational training. Even if their financial contributions are not
perceived as very large, NGOs play an important role in the development of Cambodia, working with local
communities and disadvantaged groups that are difficult to target for multilateral and bilateral donors. Some
NGOs even act as sub-contractors, or implementing partners, through which bilateral agencies channel
funds for specific purposes and activities.
Coordination of ODA
ODA has played a crucial role in Cambodia’s past five years of economic and social development.
Constraints imposed by the lack of absorptive capacity, derived from the weak base of human resources,
insufficiently developed institutional and legal frameworks, the imperfect physical infrastructure, etc., imply
a continued heavy dependence on external funding for some years to come.
In response to the challenge of coordinating the huge influx of ODA in 1994, the government set up the
Council for the Development of Cambodia (CDC). The CDC was given the very complex task of developing
an institutional framework to ensure that national resources, and external resources including ODA, were to
be used efficiently and channeled to national priority areas – sectoral and geographical. Chaired by the
Prime Minister, the CDC comprises two arms: the Cambodian Investment Board (CIB) for private sector
investments and the Cambodian Rehabilitation and Development Board (CRDB) for ODA mobilization for
public investment and technical assistance.
Much external assistance is not subject to Cambodian budgeting processes, being directly implemented by
donors, including NGOs. Similarly, line ministries still deal directly with donors. Recognizing these realities,
in 1995 the CDC/CRDB established an in-country aid coordination system. This included a data base (from
which the annual DCR is derived) and a Public Investment Management System (PIMS).
The performance to date in aid coordination has been satisfactory, in that there appear to be few, if any,
examples of obvious duplication or overlapping of efforts. However, much remains to be done to bring
donors’ – including NGOs – interventions in line with national priorities and programmes, by respecting the
CDC mechanism and, increasingly, by reflecting ODA in the national budget. The current situation of
separate accounting and reporting by and for each donor is inefficient, and places impossible demands on
government counterparts. Because of this, donors become part of the problem rather than part of the
solution.
Coordination is easier and more effective where national programmes exist. Such programmes enable
donors to integrate their inputs into a goal-related, elaborated framework and to track progress – financial
and substantive – using simple reporting and evaluation mechanisms. The Health Coverage Plan, elaborated
by the Ministry of Health is a good example of such a national programme. The intention of the Government

Dialogue between the Government and the donor community is facilitated by the Consultative Group (CG)
mechanism. The CG is now established as the principal instrument for the annual review and discussion
among the government and its main donor partners of the priorities, progress and problems of Cambodia’s
development process. It also provides the Government with an opportunity to present to donors its external
funding requirements and for donors to confirm their assistance to Cambodia.
In response to the request for regular and effective monitoring of the CG recommendations and with the
prospect of a renewed flow of external assistance to Cambodia, the Government took the initiative, following
the February 1999 meeting, of organizing in-country review meetings on a quarterly basis. Review meetings
are chaired by the Prime Minister and attended by the Cabinet and representatives of the donor community.
In parallel, a joint decision was made at the 1999 CG meeting in Tokyo to establish a regular local donor
coordination mechanism. This arrangement involves “umbrella” working groups at high level to discuss
issues of current interest and concern. In particular these working groups focus on monitoring the
performance of the government in implementing its declared policies and programmes of reform. Five
working groups have been established: fiscal reform (led by the Asian Development Bank), forestry (FAO),
social sectors (UNICEF), public administration reform (UNDP) and demobilization (World Bank). The
working groups meet in advance of the quarterly review meetings. The mechanism contributes to consensus
building on key issues of concerns in each area.
This new arrangement is expected to share the “coordination load” among the major actors and to bring
about improved coordination among donors, better integration of external assistance into national
programmes and much closer monitoring of national performances using benchmarking.
